title: 16  Workshop 5: Putting it all together
section: 16.5 Question 2: The effect of mousezempic on gene expression
text:
16.5 Question 2: The effect of mousezempic on gene expression
Our second research question was about the effect of mousezempic on the expression of the TH and PRLH genes. To answer this question, we can use the genes_tidy dataset that we prepared earlier, by pivoting the genes dataset to be longer and separating the measurement column so each variable is contained within its own column.
Let’s take a look at the genes_tidy data to remind ourselves of the information it contains. You might like to use the View() function, or just type the name of the data like so:

genes_tidy

# A tibble: 3,087 × 5
   group         id_num gene  replicate expression
   <chr>          <dbl> <chr> <chr>          <dbl>
 1 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep1           3239.
 2 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep2           5964.
 3 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep3           4123.
 4 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep1            225.
 5 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep2            359.
 6 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep3            314.
 7 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 rep1            858.
 8 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 rep2           1292.
 9 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 rep3            988.
10 grp_treatment      2 Th    rep1           2665.
# ℹ 3,077 more rows


Each mouse has a unique id_num, and belongs to a group (either treatment or control). There are also gene expression measurements in triplicate for each of three different genes: the TH and PRLH genes we are interested in and HPRT1, a housekeeping gene.

16.5.1 Do the treatment and control groups differ?
To investigate differences in gene expression between the treatment an control groups, a good first step would be to make a plot. Boxplots, violin plots or beeswarm plots would be a good choice to visualise this type of data.






ImportantPractice exercise: plotting the relationship between mousezempic and gene expression



Take a moment to think about how you could achieve this, and check your answer below. As an additional exercise, how could you prevent the HPRT1 gene from being shown on your plot?


Solution

Since we want to plot the expression of two different genes, we have a couple of options.
Firstly, we could use a single ggplot() function call, and facet the plot by the gene. However, if we want to exlude the HPRT1 gene, we’ll have to first use the filter() function from dplyr to remove it from our data frame.

genes_tidy %>%
  # remember that != is the test for inequality in R
  # also note we use Hprt1 not HPRT1: needs to match 
  # the data frame exactly for filter() to work
  filter(gene != "Hprt1") %>%
  # we will pipe this filtered data into the ggplot
  # because we are unlikely to want to re-use it
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = expression)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    # to facet write ~ then the name of the column
    # need scales = "free" because otherwise it will
    # use the same scales for both genes, and the 
    # expression levels are quite different
    facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free") +
    theme_bw()








Another option would be to plot each of TH and PRLH separately, with two different ggplot() function calls and then combine them with patchwork (make sure this package is loaded!). To do this, we would also have to use the filter() function, this time to filter to just the rows that contain the gene we want to plot

# first plot: TH
th_plot <- genes_tidy %>%
  # == tests for equality in R 
  filter(gene == "Th") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = expression)) +
    geom_boxplot() + 
    # should add a title to remind us which one this is
    labs(title = "TH gene expression in control vs treatment groups") +
    theme_bw()

# second plot: PRLH
prlh_plot <- genes_tidy %>%
  # == tests for equality in R 
  filter(gene == "Prlh") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = expression)) +
    geom_boxplot() + 
    # should add a title to remind us which one this is
    labs(
      title = "PRLH gene expression in control vs treatment groups") +
    theme_bw()

# combine them using patchwork + syntax
th_plot + prlh_plot








The first method with faceting requires less code, but the second method of making two separate plots that are combined with patchwork allows you to be more flexible with the layout and include extra plots in the figure if desired.
But either solution is perfectly valid, and allows us to see that the expression of the Th and Prlh genes is higher in the treatment group than in the control group.



R also provides a range of functions that we could use to formally test the relationship between these variables, although they are out of the scope of this course. A helpful guide on performing statistical tests in R can be found here.


16.5.2 An aside: string manipulation
Let’s now take a moment to improve the appearance of our plot from the exercise above:









In session three we learned how to change the x and y axis labels on our graph to be more informative, but how can we change the values on the axes themselves? Currently, we have ‘grp_control’ and ‘grp_treatment’, but to make the plot look more publication-ready, it would be nice if it could just say ‘Control’ and ‘Treatment’.
We can do this with the help of the stringr tidyverse package, which contains a set of functions to manipulate string (character) data in R. Being able to programatically manipulate strings is an essential tool for dealing with real-world data, particularly when you need to extract sample information from names or (as in our case) remove irrelevant characters that only take up space on plots.
Some useful functions for string manipulation include:

str_replace(string, pattern, replacement): replaces the pattern in the string with the replacement
str_extract(string, pattern): extracts the part of the string matching the pattern
str_remove(string, pattern): removes the part of the string matching the pattern

The full list of functions can be found in the stringr package documentation.






NoteUsing stringr functions on a data frame



Remember from session 2 that when we use the pipe operator %>%, it passes whatever precedes it into the function after it as the first argument. This means that the functions we use within a chain of pipes on a data frame should (generally) have a data frame as their input, and return a data frame as their output.
But stringr functions operate on character vectors (their first argument is string, as shown above), so how can we use them on our data frames? The answer is to wrap it in the mutate() function from the dplyr package, which allows us to either edit an exisiting column or create a new one based on our string manipulation.
For example, let’s say we want to change the replicate column in our genes_tidy data frame to read ‘Replicate 1’, ‘Replicate 2’, etc instead of ‘rep1’, ‘rep2’. We would do this by using the str_replace() function inside the mutate() function like so:

genes_tidy %>%
  mutate(replicate = str_replace(replicate, "rep", "Replicate "))

# A tibble: 3,087 × 5
   group         id_num gene  replicate   expression
   <chr>          <dbl> <chr> <chr>            <dbl>
 1 grp_treatment      1 Th    Replicate 1      3239.
 2 grp_treatment      1 Th    Replicate 2      5964.
 3 grp_treatment      1 Th    Replicate 3      4123.
 4 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  Replicate 1       225.
 5 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  Replicate 2       359.
 6 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  Replicate 3       314.
 7 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 Replicate 1       858.
 8 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 Replicate 2      1292.
 9 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 Replicate 3       988.
10 grp_treatment      2 Th    Replicate 1      2665.
# ℹ 3,077 more rows


This applies to lots of other functions, not just the ones from the stringr package— if you want to use a function that takes a vector as input on a column of a data frame, wrap it in the mutate() function first!


‘Patterns’ are what the stringr package will look for in your string. For example, in this case, our pattern could be grp_ because this is what we want to remove from the strings in our ‘group’ column. This is an example of a fixed pattern, where you specify exactly what string you want to find. There is also another way to write patterns, called regular expressions which allow you to, for example, remove everything before the first underscore or all numbers. These are extremely powerful, but can get a little confusing so you might like to get help from AI to write them.






ImportantCleaning up the text on our plot



Using the stringr package, remove the ‘grp_’ from the x axis labels, and then use ggplot2 functions to add other labels to the plot. Here’s an example of what this might look like:











Solution

The code that generates the plot above is:

genes_tidy %>%
  # use str_remove function to remove 'grp_' from the 
  # beginning of the group column. need to wrap it in
  # the mutate function because we are working on a 
  # column in a data frame not just on a vector 
  mutate(group = str_remove(group, "grp_")) %>%
  filter(gene != "Hprt1") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = expression)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free") +
    theme_bw() +
    # add the other labels 
    labs(
      title = "Effect of mousezempic on gene expression",
      x = "Group", 
      y = "Expression (arbitrary units)")






16.5.3 The relationship between gene expression and weight loss
The second part of research question 2 asked us to look at whether TH and/or PRLH expression is associated with the amount of weight lost by mice taking mousezempic. To do this, we will need to join the dosage and genes_tidy data frames:

combined_data <- left_join(
    genes_tidy, # the left data frame
    dosage, # the right data frame
    by = "id_num") # name of the column to join by

combined_data

# A tibble: 3,087 × 13
   group         id_num gene  replicate.x expression mouse_strain cage_number
   <chr>          <dbl> <chr> <chr>            <dbl> <chr>        <chr>      
 1 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep1             3239. CD-1         1A         
 2 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep2             5964. CD-1         1A         
 3 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep3             4123. CD-1         1A         
 4 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep1              225. CD-1         1A         
 5 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep2              359. CD-1         1A         
 6 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep3              314. CD-1         1A         
 7 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 rep1              858. CD-1         1A         
 8 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 rep2             1292. CD-1         1A         
 9 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 rep3              988. CD-1         1A         
10 grp_treatment      2 Th    rep1             2665. CD-1         1A         
# ℹ 3,077 more rows
# ℹ 6 more variables: weight_lost_g <dbl>, replicate.y <chr>, sex <chr>,
#   drug_dose_g <dbl>, tail_length_mm <dbl>, initial_weight_g <dbl>








ImportantPlotting the relationship between gene expression and weight loss



Use the combined_data data frame and your choice of ggplot2 functions to see whether there is a relationship between the expression of the TH & PRLH genes and weight lost by mice.


Solution

Since both variables are continuous, a scatterplot is a good choice to visualise their relationship. Here is some sample code:

# first plot: TH
th_plot <- combined_data %>%
  # == tests for equality in R 
  filter(gene == "Th") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = expression, y = weight_lost_g)) +
    geom_point() + 
    labs(
      x = "TH gene expression (arbitrary units)",
      y = "Weight loss (g)") +
    theme_minimal()

# second plot: PRLH
prlh_plot <- combined_data %>%
  filter(gene == "Prlh") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = expression, y = weight_lost_g)) +
    geom_point() + 
    labs(
      x = "PRLH gene expression (arbitrary units)",
      y = "Weight loss (g)") +
    theme_minimal()

# combine them using patchwork + syntax
th_plot + prlh_plot

Warning: Removed 6 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).
Removed 6 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









We can se there is no association between the expression of TH and weight lost, and the same is true for PRLH expression and weight lost. This probably makes sense, as there are many complex regulatory pathways involved in hunger.

title: 16  Workshop 5: Putting it all together
text:
16.6 Summary
Today, we’ve tried to put together all of the skills we’ve learned in this R course and use them to address some sample data analysis questions. We’ve covered:

How to break down a written research question into steps we can write code to solve
The ‘stringr’ package for string manipulation, and some of the basic ways we can use it to clean up character columns in our data frames
The overall process of data science, and how to apply it in practice to break down our research questions into a series of steps/function calls in R

Of course, a real data analysis will likely be much longer and more complex than the toy examples we have tackled today. However, we hope that it has provided you with a basic, yet versatile toolkit for transforming the messy data you will find in the wild into a neat, tidy format that you can use to explore your research questions and produce gorgeous data visualisations.

16.6.1 Practice questions
If you have time, try having a go at addressing these additional research questions that extend those covered in the main body of the session. There are many different ways to approach them, so don’t worry if yours doesn’t match exactly with the solutions.

16.6.1.1 Practice question 1: Looking more deeply into weight loss
In our first research question, we investigated the relationship between the dosage of mousezempic and the amount of weight (in g) lost by each mouse. But, is there a better way to measure weight loss than just the number of grams lost?
To start examining this, it would be helpful to know the distribution of the mices’ initial weights.






ImportantHow much do the mice weigh before taking mousezempic?



We can examine this numerically and visually. First practice your dplyr skills and use the summarise() function to calculate some sensisble summary statistics


Solution

You can achieve this using the summarise() function without grouping, as shown below. Notice that we filter out NAs in this column first with filter(), because otherwise we’d have to set na.rm = TRUE for each of the summary statistic function calls, which would be annoying:

dosage %>%
  # first remove NAs in the initial_weight_g column
  filter(!is.na(initial_weight_g)) %>%
  # then calculate summary statistics
  summarise(
    min_iw = min(initial_weight_g),
    max_iw = max(initial_weight_g),
    av_iw = mean(initial_weight_g),
    sd_iw = sd(initial_weight_g),
    med_iw = median(initial_weight_g))

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  min_iw max_iw av_iw sd_iw med_iw
   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1   32.1   59.6  43.9  5.46   44.4


This is a nice way to practice your dplyr skills, but in reality, it’s probably easier to use the summary() function that’s built into R. Note that this function operates on a vector, so you need to access the initial_weight_g column as a vector first by either using pull() or the $ syntax we covered in session 1.

# using pull():
dosage %>% pull(initial_weight_g) %>% summary()

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
  32.10   39.23   44.45   43.92   48.50   59.60       2 

# using $
summary(dosage$initial_weight_g)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
  32.10   39.23   44.45   43.92   48.50   59.60       2 



Next, let’s look at this visualling by making a histogram of the initial mice weights:


Solution

To make a histogram with ggplot2, we can use the geom_histogram() function:

ggplot(dosage, aes(x = initial_weight_g)) + 
  geom_histogram()

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.


Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









Since this plot is kind of ugly, let’s make some cosmetic changes (optional):

ggplot(dosage, aes(x = initial_weight_g)) + 
  geom_histogram(fill = "plum", colour = "white") +
  theme_bw()

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.


Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).










Looking at these results, it seems like there is a fairly wide spread of initial weights of the mice. So, could this be affecting our interpretation of the results?


It stands to reason that mice that weigh more initially would probably be able to lose more weight once they start taking mousezempic. So, what if we expressed weight loss as a percentage of the initial body weight, rather than just in grams?






ImportantExpressing weight lost as a percentage



Use the mutate() function to add a column to the dosage data frame expressing the weight lost as a percentage of the initial weight. Then, plot the relationship between the drug dosage and percentage weight lost (coloured by mouse strain) as a scatterplot. How does this differ from when we simply looked at weight loss in grams? Hint: compare the two scatterplots by placing them side-by-side with the patchwork package, as we learned in Chapter 10.


Solution

First, we need to create the percent_wl column, and we will also use the mutate function to convert grams to milligrams as we did in research question 1:

# assign to a variable so we can use this data frame later
dosage_wl_percent <- dosage %>% 
  # we can create multiple new columns in a single mutate() function call
  mutate(
    percent_wl = (weight_lost_g / initial_weight_g) * 100,
    drug_dose_mg = drug_dose_g * 1000) 

Now that we’ve added these columns, let’s make the two scatterplots and put them side by side. To do this, we need to assign the plots to variables.

# make sure the patchwork package is loaded
library(patchwork)

# the new scatterplot
scatterplot_percentage <- ggplot(dosage_wl_percent, aes(x = drug_dose_mg, y = percent_wl, colour = mouse_strain)) +
  geom_point() + 
  labs(title = "Weight lost as a percentage") +
  theme_minimal() +
  # remove the legend, since they are the same on both plots and it's a waste
  # to have it twice
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# the original scatterplot
scatterplot_grams <- ggplot(dosage_wl_percent, aes(x = drug_dose_mg, y = weight_lost_g, colour = mouse_strain)) +
  geom_point() + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Weight lost in grams")

# arrange them with patchwork
scatterplot_percentage + scatterplot_grams

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).
Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









The two plots actually look quite different! While the BALB C and CD-1 mice lost a similar amount of grams when given similar dosages of mousezempic, the CD-1 mice on average weigh less than the BALB C mice, so in terms of the percentage of body weight lost, they have lost more. How interesting!

Recall that in research question one, we also explored the effect of sex on the relationship. Try faceting the new scatterplot you created above by sex and see what happens… hint: to clearly see this new pattern, you might need to add a linear trendline with geom_smooth().


Solution


# we can use the data frame we created above (dosage_wl_percent)
dosage_wl_percent %>%
  # although ggplot2 implicitly removes NA points, a facet will still
  # be created for those mice whose sex is unknown (try commenting this)
  # line out and seeing what happens! So we should remove NAs in the sex column.
  filter(!is.na(sex)) %>% 
  # recall we can pipe data directly into ggplot(), just don't mix up your %>% and + 
  ggplot(aes(x = drug_dose_g, y = percent_wl, colour = mouse_strain)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









The trendlines for the male and female mice actually look quite different! Perhaps this is just an artefact of our relatively low sample size, but it might also be a true pattern in the data.





16.6.1.2 Practice question 2: normalising the gene expression data
Normalisation is a common step in many data analyses, as it allows us to more easily compare data across samples or experimental groups. For example, if we were to plot the expression of all genes across the three replicates:

genes_tidy %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = replicate, y = expression)) + 
    geom_boxplot() +
    theme_minimal()








We can see that replicate 2 has higher expression on average compared to replicates 1 and 3. This might skew our results if we don’t correct for it.
There are many different ways to normalise data, depending on the type, but for the sake of this question we’ll:

Calculate the average HPRT1 expression in each replicate
Divide all TH and PRLH measurements by the average HPRT1 expression calculated above

Take a moment to think about how you could achieve this, and whether it would work better on the wide or long form of the genes data frame.


Solution

It would be much easier to do with the wide form data! That’s because each individual replicate/gene measurement is split into its own column, and in general, when using the mutate function (which is what we would need to create a new column of the normalised data) we want to work on columns. This will be a great practice of our pivoting skills, turning the genes_tidy data into wide format, performing the calculation and then pivoting it back to long format for plotting.
Keep this in mind for your own analysis, while plotting is usually easier in long format, some types of data analysis/manipulation are easier in wide format. You can change between them as it suits you!







ImportantNormalising the gene expression values



Our first task is to pivot the data into wide format. To help you do this, take a look at the genes_tidy data frame, and think about what columns exist and what new ones we need to create:

genes_tidy

# A tibble: 3,087 × 5
   group         id_num gene  replicate expression
   <chr>          <dbl> <chr> <chr>          <dbl>
 1 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep1           3239.
 2 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep2           5964.
 3 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep3           4123.
 4 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep1            225.
 5 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep2            359.
 6 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep3            314.
 7 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 rep1            858.
 8 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 rep2           1292.
 9 grp_treatment      1 Hprt1 rep3            988.
10 grp_treatment      2 Th    rep1           2665.
# ℹ 3,077 more rows


Check the out the pivoting section above (Section 10.6.1) if you need a refresher on pivoting!


Solution

To do the calculation outlined above, it would be handy if each replicate of each gene was in its own column. So, our column names should come from the ‘gene’ and ‘replicate columns’ (i.e. the names_from argument should be equal to c(gene, replicate)). Inside these columns should be the gene expression values, so the values_from argument should be ‘expression’

genes_tidy %>%
  pivot_wider(
    # create new columns based on the genes and the replicates
    names_from = c(gene, replicate),
    # the values in these columns should be gene expression
    values_from = expression)

# A tibble: 343 × 11
   group id_num Th_rep1 Th_rep2 Th_rep3 Prlh_rep1 Prlh_rep2 Prlh_rep3 Hprt1_rep1
   <chr>  <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
 1 grp_…      1   3239.   5964.   4123.      225.      359.      314.       858.
 2 grp_…      2   2665.   4867.   4240.      253.      460.      358.       709.
 3 grp_…      3   1536.   2501.   2054.      367.      552.      448.       975.
 4 grp_…      4   2732.   4800.   3981.      258.      411.      339.       725.
 5 grp_…      5   2384.   3460.   3115.      347.      651.      491.       896.
 6 grp_…      6   2972.   4880.   4028.      303.      456.      377.       865.
 7 grp_…      7   1936.   3666.   2964.      302.      441.      355.       625.
 8 grp_…      8   2801.   4977.   3795.      246.      424.      321.       856.
 9 grp_…      9   3239.   5198.   3930.      385.      654.      508.       623.
10 grp_…     10   2665.   3820.   2958.      230.      391.      301.       740.
# ℹ 333 more rows
# ℹ 2 more variables: Hprt1_rep2 <dbl>, Hprt1_rep3 <dbl>



Now that the data is in wide format, we can create the normalised columns:


Solution

We create new normalised columns that are calculated by dividing the regular column by the mean of HPRT expression in that replicate:

# save in a variable so we can use for plotting later
normalised_data <- genes_tidy %>%
  # first pivot
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = c(gene, replicate),
    values_from = expression) %>%
  # then mutate. recall we need to find the average HPRT expression
  # and then divide the other genes by that
  mutate(
    Th_rep1_norm = Th_rep1 / mean(Hprt1_rep1),
    Prlh_rep1_norm = Prlh_rep1 / mean(Hprt1_rep1),
    Th_rep2_norm = Th_rep2 / mean(Hprt1_rep2),
    Prlh_rep2_norm = Prlh_rep2 / mean(Hprt1_rep2),
    Th_rep3_norm = Th_rep3 / mean(Hprt1_rep3),
    Prlh_rep3_norm = Prlh_rep3 / mean(Hprt1_rep3)
  )




Now that we’ve normalised the data, let’s revist our second research question: does mousezempic change gene expression?






ImportantDoes normalising the data affect the relationship between mousezempic and gene expression?



First, we need to take the wide data frame we created above and pivot it into a long form that is suitable for plotting (hint: remove the non-normalised gene expression columns first with the select() function). Then, we can make the boxplot as above.


Solution

There are many different approaches we could use to pivot our normalised data into long format. Regardless of the approach, the first thing we need to do is to remove the non-normalised gene expression columns, because they will make it hard to pivot. Then, we need to pivot it longer, somehow separating the gene name and replicate into their own columns.
This can be done by using the separate function, as we learned earlier:

long_normalised_data <- normalised_data %>%
  # remove the original expression values: we don't need them and they'll
  # make pivoting difficult
  select(group, id_num, contains("norm")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    # pivot all columns containing the string 'norm'
    cols = contains("norm"),
    names_to = "measurement",
    values_to = "rel_expression") %>%
  separate(
      measurement, 
      # NA tells the separate function to discard the last bit ('norm')
      # you don't need to use it, but it's better to explicitly write that
      # you want to exclude that portion
      into = c("gene", "replicate", NA), 
      sep = "_")

Here’s a slightly more advanced way to do this, using the names_sep argument of pivot_longer() to separate the column names by underscore and place each part in its own column (so we can split up the gene name and replicate, without needing to use the separate()) function:

normalised_data %>%
  # remove the original expression values: we don't need them and they'll
  # make pivoting difficult
  select(group, id_num, contains("norm")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    # pivot all columns containing the string 'norm'
    cols = contains("norm"),
    # the first part of the column name is the gene, the second is the replicate
    # and the final part is just 'norm' to indicate its normalised. this is redundant
    # so we can use NA to tell dplyr to discard it
    names_to = c("gene", "replicate", NA),
    names_sep = "_"
  )

# A tibble: 2,058 × 5
   group         id_num gene  replicate value
   <chr>          <dbl> <chr> <chr>     <dbl>
 1 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep1      4.29 
 2 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep1      0.299
 3 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep2      4.74 
 4 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep2      0.285
 5 grp_treatment      1 Th    rep3      4.11 
 6 grp_treatment      1 Prlh  rep3      0.313
 7 grp_treatment      2 Th    rep1      3.53 
 8 grp_treatment      2 Prlh  rep1      0.335
 9 grp_treatment      2 Th    rep2      3.87 
10 grp_treatment      2 Prlh  rep2      0.366
# ℹ 2,048 more rows


Once the data is pivoted, it can then be plotted:

long_normalised_data %>%
  # as before, we'll use the str_remove function to clean up the
  # treatment/control labels on our plot
  mutate(group = str_remove(group, "grp_")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = rel_expression)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free") +
    theme_bw() +
    # add the other labels 
    labs(
      title = "Effect of mousezempic on gene expression",
      x = "Group", 
      y = "Expression (arbitrary units, relative to housekeeping gene)")








It looks like the shift in gene expression in mice taking mousezempic remains even after normalisation of the data. However, some of the outliers have now disappeared which makes the boxplot look a bit cleaner.

title: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control
text:
18.1 Setup
In today’s tutorial, we will learn how to use git and GitHub to perform version control for analyses in RStudio.
Setting up git and GitHub can take a little time at first, but once it’s done, working with them is fairly easy. If you have any trouble with the setup in this section, please let a tutor know.
crumbs: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control

title: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control
text:
18.1.1 Installing git
Before we can start using version control, we first need to make sure git is installed on your computer.






NoteTerminal vs Console



Some of the commands we’ll need to run today belong in the terminal, as opposed to the R console. You can find the terminal in the tab next to the console:



The terminal in RStudio is located in a tab next to the console


The difference between them is that the R console is for R code and output, while the terminal is a command-line interface to your computer, beyond just R. Using the terminal, you can run software, copy/create/delete files and folders, etc. just like you can using your operating system’s graphical interface. Because git is a program separate to R, we need to run git commands through the terminal.


To check whether you already have git installed, open up the Terminal tab in RStudio (next to the Console tab) and type:

git --version

If git is installed, you’ll see something like git version 2.39.2 printed out.
If you get an error, git is not installed. Install it from the git website, restart RStudio, and try running git --version again to confirm that the installation worked.






NoteTelling git who you are



Git likes to know who is making changes, so it can keep track of who did what in a project’s history. The first time you use git, you should tell it your name and email address by running these lines in the terminal (not the Console!):

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"

You only need to do this once per computer.




18.1.2 Creating a GitHub account and PAT
Git manages version control on our own computer (known as local), but to share our work and collaborate with others we need a place to store our repositories online (known as remote). This is where GitHub comes in: it’s a website that hosts git repositories, and is the most widely used platform for this in both industry and academia. There are other options like gitlab or bitbucket, but, GitHub is by far the most popular.
If you don’t already have one, head to github.com and sign up for a free account. Try to choose a professional username, as this is something future collaborators or employers will see!






TipGitHub Education



While you’re at it, consider registering for GitHub Education using your student email. This gives you free access to extra features, like GitHub Copilot (AI tool for coding).


Once you have an account, we need one more thing before RStudio and GitHub can talk to each other: a Personal Access Token (PAT). The PAT is like a password that’s specifically for letting other programs (like RStudio) act on your behalf on GitHub.
To create a PAT, follow this link and give your token a name and expiration date:



Choose a name and expiration date for your PAT


What you’re supposed to do is have multiple PAT for each task you do, each with its own expiry date (e.g. one for this subject, that expires at the end of the semester). Personally, I just have one PAT that has no expiration that I use for everything. This is not good practice, but I don’t put anything on GitHub that I’m not comfortable with being public (e.g. commercially-sensitive research data) and I’m certainly not important enough for someone to want to hack into my GitHub and do anything nefarious. Do what you’re comfortable with.
Once you’ve set those, scroll down and click Generate token.






WarningCopy your token somewhere safe!



GitHub will only show you the token once on the next screen:



I already deleted this one, so don’t bother trying to use it!


Copy it immediately, as you won’t be able to view it again (although you can always generate a new one if you lose it).


Once you have your token copied, go back to RStudio and run:

# first install gitcreds package
install.packages("gitcreds")
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()

# note about the ::
# package_name::function() is an alternative way to access
# functions from packages, without needing to use library(package_name)

You’ll be prompted to paste in your PAT, and you shouldn’t need to do this again as RStudio will remember it.
crumbs: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control

title: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control
text:
18.2 Creating your first ‘repo’
Fun fact: most people just call repositories ‘repos’ for short.

18.2.1 Using GitHub to make a repository
Now that git and GitHub are set up, let’s create somewhere for our analysis to live! Head to github.com/new (make sure you’re logged in) and you should see a page like this:



To create a new repository, just give it a name, description and choose whether it should be public or private


You’ll need to fill in a few details, as shown above:

Repository name: choose something short and descriptive, without spaces (this is similar to how we name our variables, see Section 4.3). For this exercise, you might like to call yours something like mousezempic-analysis or biol90042-test. The name needs to be unique to your GitHub account, but it’s ok for two different people to have the same repository name.
Public or private: public repositories can be seen by anyone, while private ones are only visible to you and people you invite. I usually make my repositories public, unless I’m still working on them/they’re really messy. Public repositories are a great way to share your analysis code with the wider scientific community (e.g. for your thesis or a publication) and if you are interested in pursuing bioinformatics further, potential supervisors or employers often like to look through your GitHub.
Add a README file: tick this box. A README is a file (usually written in a format called Markdown, which is a little bit like quarto) that describes what your repository is about, and it’s good practice to always include one

Once you’re happy, click Create repository.


18.2.2 Linking your repository to a new R project
We now have an empty repository sitting on GitHub (remote), but we need to bring a copy down onto our own computer (local) so we can actually work on it. This process is called ‘cloning’.
Conveniently, RStudio lets us create a brand new R project directly from a GitHub repository, so we don’t need to use terminal commands:

On your repository’s GitHub page, click the green ’Code’ button and copy the URL under the HTTPS tab:



Click on the green code button to copy the URL


In RStudio, go to ’File’ > ‘New Project’ > ‘Version Control’ > ‘Git’



Create a new R project from the top-right hand corner of RStudio





Choose the ‘version control’ option to make a new project





Choose ‘git’


Paste the URL into the ‘Repository URL’ field, give the directory a name and choose where you want to put it on your computer. Then click’Create Project’



Paste the URL from your GitHub



RStudio will open a new session with your project, and you should notice a new tab called ‘Git’ has appeared alongside the Environment and History tabs:



The ‘Git’ panel in RStudio


This is our git interface, and we’ll be using it a lot for the rest of this tutorial!
crumbs: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control

title: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control
text:
18.3 Let’s do some analysis!
Now that our repository is set up, let’s actually write some code to track! Create a new R script and save it inside your project.
We’ll revisit the mousezempic dosage data that we’ve been using in this course, and try to answer the following question: does the amount of weight lost by mice increase as the dosage of mousezempic increases, and is this relationship affected by mouse strain or sex?
First, let’s load the tidyverse package and read in the data (since we aren’t in the usual R project we use in the workshops, let’s just read it in from the internet, with the URL)

library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

# you can read in files from the internet by providing the URL to them instead of a file path on your computer
dosage <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WEHI-Education/BIOL90042_R_Course/refs/heads/main/data/mousezempic_dosage_data.csv")

Rows: 344 Columns: 9
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (4): mouse_strain, cage_number, replicate, sex
dbl (5): weight_lost_g, drug_dose_g, tail_length_mm, initial_weight_g, id_num

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


To answer this question, let’s start by making a scatterplot:

dosage %>%
  # first convert drug_dose_g into mg
  # to make it easier to read
  mutate(dose_mg = drug_dose_g * 10000) %>%
  # now make a scatterplot
  ggplot(aes(x = dose_mg, y = weight_lost_g, colour = mouse_strain)) +
    geom_point() +
    # nicer colour palette
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#ab2929", "#73b7bd", "#ccd65c")) +
    # theme and labels
    theme_classic() +
    labs(
      x = "Drug dosage (mg)",
      y = "Weight lost (mg)",
      colour = "Mouse strain",
      title = "Relationship between drug dosage and weight lost"
      )

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









We’ve written some code and made a nice plot, but right now, this only exists on your own computer. If your laptop died tomorrow, this important analysis would be lost! Backing up your scripts to GitHub is a handy way to protect against this, along with the benefits of being able to share them with others.
crumbs: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control

title: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control
text:
18.4 Adding and committing your changes

18.4.1 Add files
Look at the Git tab in RStudio. You should see your R script there, with a yellow question mark icon next to it. This means the file is ‘untracked’: git has noticed it exists, but isn’t yet keeping an eye on its changes.



Untracked files in the git panel


To tell git we want to keep track of these files, we need to ‘add’ (also known as ‘stage’) them. You can do this by ticking the checkbox next to your file’s name in the Git tab, and the icon should change to a green ‘A’ (for ‘added’):



After adding your files, the icon will change to an ‘A’








NoteWhy do we need to ‘add’ files?



You might wonder why git makes us tick a checkbox instead of just tracking every file automatically. This process lets you choose exactly which changes should be bundled together into a single commit. For example, if you made changes to two totally unrelated files, you might want to save them as two separate commits with two different messages, rather than lumping them together. This gives you much finer control over your project’s history.




18.4.2 Commit changes
Once your file is staged, click the ‘Commit’ button. A new window will pop up showing you the changes that are about to be committed. This is called a ‘diff’, and lines you’ve added will be shown in green, while lines you’ve deleted will be shown in red.
In the box in the top right, write a short, descriptive ‘commit message’ that explains what exactly you’ve changed. For example: ‘Added scatterplot of dosage vs weight loss’.



In the commit window, you can view your changes and write a commit message








WarningWrite good commit messages!



It can be tempting to write vague/lazy commit messages like “updates” or “fixed errors”, but future you (or your collaborators) will thank you for being descriptive! A good commit message briefly explains (in a sentence) what changed and, if it’s not obvious, why.


Once you’ve written your message, click ‘commit’. You’ve now made your first commit! You can see a record of all your commits by clicking the ‘history’ button (the clock icon) in the Git tab.
crumbs: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control

title: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control
text:
18.5 Pushing changes to the remote
So far, our commit only exists on our own computer (the local repository). To back it up and share it, we need to send our commits to GitHub (the remote repository). This is called ‘pushing’.
In the Git tab, simply click the ‘push’ button (green up arrow):



Click on the green arrow to push your commits to the remote


Head back to your repository’s page on GitHub and refresh it: you should see your R script sitting there, along with your commit message:



Your commit should now show up on GitHub








ImportantPractice exercise: make another commit



Try making a small change to your R script (for example, add a comment, or change the colours in scale_colour_manual()). Then, add, commit and push this change, following the same steps as above. Remember to save your R script before adding, otherwise your change won’t be tracked!
Afterwards, look at the ‘history’ button in the Git tab, and the commit history on GitHub. Can you see both of your commits listed?


Congratulations, you have now completed the basic git workflow in RStudio!






NoteGoing from an R project to a GitHub repo



Sometimes you’ll already have an R project on your computer that you want to turn into a git repository and put onto GitHub (i.e. the reverse of starting from a new one on GitHub, like we just did). The easiest way to achieve this is using the usethis package:
With your existing project open in RStudio, run:

# install usethis first
install.packages("usethis")
usethis::use_git()

This initialises (sets up) git for your project. Then, add your files and commit, as you have learned above.
Once you’re ready, run:

usethis::use_github()

This will create a brand new repository on your GitHub account and link it to your local project, all in one step!
crumbs: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control

title: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control
text:
18.6 Branches
So far, we’ve been working directly on our project’s main branch, which is where you always start by default. But what if we want to try out a new idea, without risking breaking the version of our analysis that’s already working? This is where branches come in: they let us create a separate, parallel version of our project to experiment in, which we can later bring back together with our main work (or discard, if things don’t work out). They’re also handy for working with others, but we’ll cover that later.

18.6.1 Let’s take a different approach to the analysis!
So far, we’ve been considering the weight loss of mice in absolute amounts (i.e. the total number of grams that they lost), but the mice had a range of different initial weights. In this section, we’ll instead represent weight loss as a percentage of each mouse’s initial body weight, and repeat our analysis to see if anything changes.
First, we’ll create a new branch. In the git tab, click the branch icon (purple, ‘L’ shaped) in the top right corner.



The git branch button in RStudio


Give your new branch a short, descriptive name, like percentage-approach, and make sure ‘Sync branch with remote’ is ticked, then click ‘create’.



Name your branch something informative


RStudio will automatically switch you onto this new branch, but you can always check which branch you’re currently on in the Git tab, the branch name is next to the branch button.
Now, let’s perform our alternative analysis. We can create a percentage weight loss column using mutate, and I’ll also facet the plot by sex this time too:

dosage %>%
  # first convert drug_dose_g into mg
  # to make it easier to read
  mutate(dose_mg = drug_dose_g * 10000) %>%
  mutate(percent_wl = (weight_lost_g / initial_weight_g) * 100) %>%
  # now make a scatterplot
  ggplot(aes(x = dose_mg, y = percent_wl, colour = mouse_strain)) +
  geom_point() +
  # nicer colour palette
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#ab2929", "#73b7bd", "#ccd65c")) +
  # theme and labels
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Drug dosage (mg)",
    y = "Weight lost (mg)",
    colour = "Mouse strain",
    title = "Relationship between drug dosage and weight lost"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~sex)

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Just like before, add and commit this change, then push to send your new branch to the remote repo on GitHub.


18.6.2 Merging your branch back
Now we have two versions of our analysis: our original scatterplot on the main branch, and our updated percentage weight loss version on the percent-approach branch. Let’s say we decide we like this new approach, and want to make it the main version of our analysis (i.e. put it on the main branch) this is called ‘merging’.
An easy and well-organised way to do this is through GitHub, using what’s called a ‘Pull Request’ (abbreviated to PR). A pull request is essentially a proposal to merge the changes from one branch into another, and it gives you (or your collaborators) a chance to review changes before they become a permanent part of the project.
On your repository’s GitHub page, you should see a prompt asking if you’d like to create a pull request for your recently pushed branch:



After you push a new branch, GitHub prompts you to create a PR


Click ‘Compare & pull request’, add a short description of your changes, and click ‘Create pull request’:



You can add descriptions of why you think your changes are good/important


On the following page, you can review the PR one more time, then click ‘Merge pull request’ to bring your changes into the main branch:



After creating the PR, you need to review it and accept it








NoteMerge conflicts



Sometimes, if two branches have both changed the same lines of the same file, git won’t know which version to keep, and you’ll get a ‘merge conflict’. Don’t panic if this happens! Git will mark the conflicting sections directly in your file, and you just need to manually edit it to decide which changes (or a combination of both) you want to keep, then stage and commit the result. The conflicted sections are marked with conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>).


Once merged, don’t forget to switch back to the main branch in RStudio (using the dropdown in the Git tab) and click ‘Pull’ (blue downwards-pointing arrow). If you read the popup, you’ll notice that this brings the recently-merged changes down onto your computer:



After pulling the main branch, we now have these changes in our local repo
crumbs: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control

title: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control
text:
18.7 Collaborating with others
One of the biggest advantages of GitHub is how it lets multiple people work on the same project together. This may be useful for your final project.

18.7.1 Adding someone to your git repo
The first thing you need to do is give your collaborator(s) access. On your repository’s GitHub page, go to ‘Settings’ > ’Collaborators’, then click’Add people’ and search for your classmate’s GitHub username:



Add collaborators through the repo settings


They’ll receive an invitation via email (or a notification on GitHub) which they’ll need to accept before they can push changes to your repository. Note that even if your repository is public, anyone can view and clone it, but they’ll still need to be added as a collaborator to push changes directly.


18.7.2 Working on a repo with multiple people
Once you have accepted an invite to someone’s repository, you should clone it onto your own computer (following the same steps we used earlier).
Test it out now with a friend!






ImportantPractice exercise: collaborating on an analysis



With a partner, try the following:

Both of you should make a small, different change somewhere in the script (for example, one person changes the plot title, while the other adds a new comment) and commit these changes locally
Whoever commits and pushes first will have no trouble. But when the second person tries to push, they should get an error, because the remote history has moved on since they last synced!
To fix this, the second person needs to pull first, to bring down the latest changes from GitHub, before trying to push again

If you were both editing completely different parts of the file, git will usually be able to automatically combine (‘merge’) both sets of changes for you. But if you happened to edit the exact same lines, you’ll encounter a merge conflict, just like we mentioned above! It’s usually good practice to agree with your collaborator to work on different parts of the file, and make sure to pull changes often.


Working collaboratively on the same files takes a bit of practice, but a few habits will make your life much easier:

Pull before you start working, and again before you push, to make sure you have everyone else’s latest changes
Commit and push often, in small chunks, rather than making one giant commit at the end of the day
Communicate with your collaborators about who is working on what, to minimise the chances of conflicting changes in the first place

With these habits in place, git and GitHub become a really powerful way to collaborate on data analysis projects, whether that’s with a couple of classmates or an entire research team!






NoteFurther git resources



We’ve only scratched the surface of git and GitHub today! If you’d like to go further, here are a couple of great resources:

Happy Git with R is a fantastic, R-specific guide that covers everything we’ve done today (and more) in much greater depth
If you’re keen to learn to use git from the command line rather than through RStudio’s interface, the Software Carpentry git novice lesson is a great place to start

As with any coding skill, the best way to get comfortable with git is to keep using it, so try to use this for the final project if you can!
crumbs: 18  Tutorial 7: Using git and GitHub for version control

title: 19  Workshop 6: Statistics in R
text:
19.1 Testing associations between categorical variables
So far in BIOL90042, we’ve learnt how to identify patterns in our data by examining descriptive/summary statistics (mean, median etc) and visualising it with various plot types. In this workshop, we will learn how to formally test whether these patterns are statistically significant, using R. We will start by talking about how to check the assumptions behind a statistical test, then work through various different types of tests, as well as linear regression. We’ll also see how the ggpubr package can help us visualise many of these tests directly on a plot.
Please note that this is not a statistics subject, so this workshop will skip over most of the mathematics underlying these tests. If you’re interested, a nice overview can be found in the Learning Statistics With R ebook.
Today, we’ll use a few extra packages, which you’ll need to install. These are:
Once you’ve got them installed, don’t forget to load them with the library() function:
Finally, we need to read in the mousezempic dosage data we’ve been working with so far this semester. As a practice exercise, have a go at doing this yourself!
The first type of test we will cover is that of associations between categorical variables. This will allow us to answer questions such as ‘is there a systematic association between mouse strain and sex in our mousezempic study?’

title: 19  Workshop 6: Statistics in R
text:
19.1.1 Chi-squared test
The chi-squared (\(\chi^2\)) test of independence compares the observed frequency of every combination of two categorical variables against the frequency we would expect if the two variables were completely unrelated (independent).
In other words it tests the following hypotheses:

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): the two categorical variables are independent (no association)
Alternate hypothesis (\(H_1\)): the two categorical variables are associated

Before perfomring any statistical test, we need to first consider the assumptions of that test and ensure our data conforms to these. The assumptions of the (\(\chi^2\)) test are as follows:






WarningAssumptions of the (\(\chi^2\)) test




Observations are independent of one another (each mouse is only counted once, and they do not influence each other)
The categories of each variable are mutually exclusive and exhaustive (every mouse falls into exactly one strain and one sex)
Expected cell counts are reasonably large — a common rule of thumb is that no more than 20% of cells should have an expected count below 5. When this is violated (e.g. for small or sparse tables), use fisher.test() instead, which computes an exact p value.

You can generally account for these assumptions in your study design.


In order to conduct a (\(\chi^2\)) test, the first thing we need to do is construct a contingency table, that counts up the number of observations for every combination of our two categorical variables. In workshop 3, we discussed how to do this using pivot_wider() (see Section 10.6.1.1), mostly as an exercise to explain how to use that function.
However, there is an easier way, using the base R function table(). Note that, for base R functions, we need to access the column names with $, as we did in workshop 1 (see Section 4.6.3).

# assign it to a variable, we'll need this
# later to do the test
strain_sex_table <- table(dosage$mouse_strain, dosage$sex)

# view the table
strain_sex_table

        
         female male
  BALBc      34   34
  Black6     58   61
  CD1        73   73


As we can see, the counts in every cell are comfortably above 5, so a (\(\chi^2\)) test is appropriate here.
You may also notice that the proportion of male and female mice looks very similar across all three strains, suggesting there may be no association between strain and sex. Let’s still do the (\(\chi^2\)) test though, to learn how it works. We can do this using the chisq.test() function:

chisq.test(strain_sex_table)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  strain_sex_table
X-squared = 0.048607, df = 2, p-value = 0.976


The test statistic is very small (0.05) and the p value (0.98) is far greater than 0.05, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis.
We can therefore conclude that there is no evidence of an association between mouse strain and sex in our dosage data, which is consistent with sex being allocated at random with respect to strain as we would hope for a well-designed experiment.






ImportantPractice exercises



Try these practice questions to test your understanding!

1. We want to know whether mice were allocated evenly across the three experimental replicates (replicate), regardless of mouse_strain. Which line of code correctly generates the contingency table we would need to answer this?




 ✔table(dosage$mouse_strain, dosage$replicate)


 ✗table(dosage$replicate)


 ✗chisq.test(dosage$mouse_strain, dosage$replicate)


 ✗pivot_wider(dosage, mouse_strain, replicate)






2. Suppose the contingency table above has an expected count of 3 in one of its cells. What should we do?




 ✗Nothing, the (\(\chi^2\)) test doesn’t have any assumptions about cell counts


 ✗Remove that cell from the table before running chisq.test()


 ✔Use fisher.test() instead, since the (\(\chi^2\)) approximation may not be reliable with such a small expected count


 ✗Increase the sample size of just that cell







Solutions


table(dosage$mouse_strain, dosage$replicate) builds a contingency table cross-tabulating the counts of every combination of mouse_strain and replicate, which is what we need before running a (\(\chi^2\)) test.
An expected cell count of 3 is below our rule-of-thumb threshold of 5, so the (\(\chi^2\)) approximation may be unreliable here. fisher.test() calculates an exact p value instead and doesn’t rely on this large-sample approximation.






19.1.2 Fisher’s exact test
So far, our examples from the dosage data have had a large enough sample size that the assumptions of our (\(\chi^2\)) test are met. This means we haven’t had a chance to use fisher.test() yet, so let’s create some dummy data to try it out. Imagine a small pilot experiment: 10 knockout mice and 10 wildtype mice were each given mousezempic, and we recorded whether each one responded to treatment.
These results are given in a matrix (we’ll learn more about matrices in workshop 7):

pilot_table <- matrix(
  c(8, 2,
    3, 7),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    genotype = c("knockout", "wildtype"),
    response = c("responder", "non_responder")
  )
)

pilot_table

          response
genotype   responder non_responder
  knockout         8             2
  wildtype         3             7


With only 20 mice split across four cells, several expected counts here will fall below 5, so the (\(\chi^2\)) test isn’t appropriate. R will actually warn us about this if we try to use it:

chisq.test(pilot_table)

Warning in chisq.test(pilot_table): Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect



    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  pilot_table
X-squared = 3.2323, df = 1, p-value = 0.0722


Instead, we should use fisher.test(), which calculates an exact p value based on the hypergeometric distribution, rather than relying on a large-sample approximation:

fisher.test(pilot_table)


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  pilot_table
p-value = 0.06978
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
   0.8821175 127.0558418
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
  8.153063 


Notice that this one doesn’t give any warnings.

title: 19  Workshop 6: Statistics in R
text:
19.2 Comparing means: t-test and ANOVA
Another very common statistical task is testing whether a continuous outcome differs between groups. For example, does weight_lost_g differ between male and female mice, or between mouse strains?






WarningAssumptions of the t-test and ANOVA




Observations are independent of one another
The outcome is approximately normally distributed within each group (rather than in the dataset overall). If not, use a non-parametric test like wilcox.test() or kruskal.test()
The groups have approximately equal variance. If not, use Welch’s correction: t.test(var.equal = FALSE) or oneway.test()




19.2.1 Comparing two groups: the t-test
Let’s use a t-test to determine whether weight_lost_g differs between male and female mice.
First, it’s always a good idea to visualise the data:

ggplot(dosage, aes(x = sex, y = weight_lost_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  # set ylim to 0 so as not to magnify small differences
  ylim(0, 6.5)








Looking at the plot, it seems like there might be a slight difference, and the variances appear fairly similar
Let’s now check the normality assumption, using a QQ-plot for each group. A QQ (quantile-quantile) plot compares the quantiles of our data against the quantiles we would expect if the data was perfectly normally distributed. We can make a QQ-plot using ggplot2 with geom_qq(), adding a reference line with geom_qq_line() to make it easier to judge how similar our data is to the normal distribution:

ggplot(dosage, aes(sample = weight_lost_g)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  # facet because we need to check normality for each group
  facet_wrap(~sex)








If our data were normally distributed, the points would sit neatly along the diagonal reference line.
Both groups show a distinct curve away from the straight reference line, which suggests weight_lost_g is not normally distributed in either group.
We can confirm this with a Shapiro-Wilk test (using shapiro.test()) in each group:

dosage %>%
  filter(sex == "male") %>%
  # shapiro.test() needs a vector, so use pull()
  pull(weight_lost_g) %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.92504, p-value = 1.227e-07

dosage %>%
  filter(sex == "female") %>%
  pull(weight_lost_g) %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.91931, p-value = 6.155e-08


Both p values are far below 0.05, so we reject normality in both groups.
This means a t-test isn’t actually valid here (we should use the non-parametric alternative wilcox.test() instead), but for the sake of showing you how one works in R, let’s run it anyway. We can compare this to the non-parametric test in a minute.
To run a t-test in R, use the t.test() function, and provide it three arguments:

A formula of the format y ~ x (outcome ~ grouping variable)
data, the dataframe that contains columns y and x from the formula
var.equal = TRUE for a Student’s t-test (assuming variances are equal) or var.equal = FALSE for Welch’s t-test (assuming variances are not equal)


t.test(
  weight_lost_g ~ sex, # compare weight lost across sex
  data = dosage, # use dosage data
  var.equal = TRUE # student t-test
  )


    Two Sample t-test

data:  weight_lost_g by sex
t = -8.5417, df = 331, p-value = 4.897e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group female and group male is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.8408014 -0.5260222
sample estimates:
mean in group female   mean in group male 
            3.862273             4.545685 


The p value (4.90e-16) is much smaller than 0.05, suggesting (as the output says), that there is a difference in the mean amount of weight lost by female and male mice. This is not unexpected: we know that male mice weigh more to begin with, so they therefore have more weight to lose than female mice.


19.2.2 Comparing more than two groups: ANOVA
The t-test only compares two groups, so while we could use it to compare male vs female mice, if we want to compare weight_lost_g across all three mouse strains at once, we need its multi-group extension: the ANOVA (analysis of variance). Rather than comparing two means directly, ANOVA compares the variance between groups to the variance within groups, to test whether at least one group mean differs from the others.
Again, let’s begin by visualising what we are about to test:

ggplot(dosage, aes(x = mouse_strain, y = weight_lost_g)) +
  geom_boxplot()








Note that, just like for the t-test, ANOVA assumes our continuous variable is approximately normally distributed (which we can check using a QQ-plot or Shapiro-Wilks test):

# make a qq plot
ggplot(dosage, aes(sample = initial_weight_g)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  # facet because we need to check normality for each group
  facet_wrap(~mouse_strain)







# shapiro-wilks test
dosage %>%
  filter(mouse_strain == "BALBc") %>%
  # shapiro.test() needs a vector, so use pull()
  pull(weight_lost_g) %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.98449, p-value = 0.5605

dosage %>%
  filter(mouse_strain == "Black6") %>%
  pull(weight_lost_g) %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.98606, p-value = 0.2605

dosage %>%
  filter(mouse_strain == "CD1") %>%
  pull(weight_lost_g) %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.98116, p-value = 0.04232


This time, we’re actually only violating the normality assumption for the CD1 strain (p value 0.04)! We’ll compare the result to a the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallace test later, but for now let’s proceed with the ANOVA:
We can perform an ANOVA in R using the aov() function, with the same y ~ x formula notation we used for the t-test:

aov(weight_lost_g ~ mouse_strain, data = dosage)

Call:
   aov(formula = weight_lost_g ~ mouse_strain, data = dosage)

Terms:
                mouse_strain Residuals
Sum of Squares     145.19022  70.06945
Deg. of Freedom            2       330

Residual standard error: 0.4607946
Estimated effects may be unbalanced


Although the way we use the aov() function is quite similar to t.test(), the output looks very different! We can’t see a p-value anywhere. This is because, statistically, ANOVAs are a special case of a linear model (see Section 19.5) and so the output of the aov() function inherits some quirks from how linear models are reported in R.
To find the p-value and answer our question, we can pass this to the summary() function:

aov(weight_lost_g ~ mouse_strain, data = dosage) %>% summary()

              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
mouse_strain   2 145.19   72.60   341.9 <2e-16 ***
Residuals    330  70.07    0.21                   
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The p value is extremely small, so we conclude that weight_lost_g differs between at least one pair of strains. This matches our observation from the boxplot above, where Black-6 mice visibly lost more weight than BALBc or CD1 mice.
We can also get a tidy version of this table with the tidy() function from the broom package:

aov(weight_lost_g ~ mouse_strain, data = dosage) %>% tidy()

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  term            df sumsq meansq statistic   p.value
  <chr>        <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 mouse_strain     2 145.  72.6        342.  3.74e-81
2 Residuals      330  70.1  0.212       NA  NA       


This could be useful if, for example, we wanted to extract the p value and use this in further R code (e.g. to label a plot).






TipWhich pairs of groups differ?



A significant ANOVA (or Kruskal-Wallis) result only tells us that one group differs from another, but it doesn’t say which pair(s). We can find this by performing what’s known as a ‘post-hoc pairwise test’ (e.g. Tukey’s HSD (honest significant difference) test):

aov(weight_lost_g ~ mouse_strain, data = dosage) %>% TukeyHSD()

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = weight_lost_g ~ mouse_strain, data = dosage)

$mouse_strain
                    diff        lwr        upr    p adj
Black6-BALBc  1.35934874  1.1944304  1.5242671 0.000000
CD1-BALBc    -0.02692385 -0.1862005  0.1323528 0.916431
CD1-Black6   -1.38627259 -1.5202554 -1.2522897 0.000000


This shows us that there is a statistically significant difference between Black-6 and BALBc mice, as well as betwen CD-1 and Black-6 mice, but not between CD-1 and BALBc mice, which matches our observations in the boxplot above.


Unlike for t.test(), the aov() function doesn’t have an argument for equal variances. If your variances aren’t equal, you need to instead use the oneway.test() function, which does have this argument:

oneway.test(weight_lost_g ~ mouse_strain, data = dosage, var.equal = FALSE)


    One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances)

data:  weight_lost_g and mouse_strain
F = 316.5, num df = 2.00, denom df = 187.68, p-value < 2.2e-16




19.2.3 Non-parametric tests
When a parametric assumption (i.e. normality) is badly violated, we can turn to a non-parametric alternative instead. These tests don’t assume the outcome is normally distributed and instead test for differences in the ranks of the data.






WarningAssumptions of the Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis tests




Observations are independent of one another
The outcome variable is at least ordinal (i.e. it can be meaningfully ranked)
If you want to interpret the result as a difference in medians specifically (rather than just ‘the distributions differ’), the groups should have similarly shaped distributions



Non-parametric tests are more robust to outliers and skewed distributions than their parametric counterparts, but they can be somewhat less powerful to detect a true effect when the data are actually normally distributed. Therefore, you should only use them when you really need to.

19.2.3.1 The Wilcoxon rank-sum test
The Wilcoxon rank-sum test (also called the Mann-Whitney test when applied on two samples, like we will do here) is the non-parametric equivalent of the t-test we covered earlier. Instead of comparing means, it tests whether one group tends to have overall higher or lower ranked values than the other.
Let’s revisit our comparison of weight_lost_g between male and female mice. We can use it by simply replacing t.test() with wilcox.test()

wilcox.test(weight_lost_g ~ sex, data = dosage)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  weight_lost_g by sex
W = 6874.5, p-value = 1.813e-15
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


The p value is again far smaller than 0.05, so both tests agree here: male and female mice differ in weight lost.


19.2.3.2 The Kruskal-Wallis test
The just like the t-test, the Wilcoxon test only compares two groups. The non-parametric version of the ANOVA we ran above is called the Kruskal-Wallis test, and we can run it using the kruskal.test() function:

kruskal.test(weight_lost_g ~ mouse_strain, data = dosage)


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  weight_lost_g by mouse_strain
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 212.09, df = 2, p-value < 2.2e-16








ImportantPractice exercises



Try these practice questions to test your understanding!

1. If you check the normality assumption for a continuous variable in two groups using a QQ plot and Shapiro-Wilk test, and find that the assumption is clearly violated in both groups, which test should you use to compare them?




 ✗t.test(), since it’s the standard test for comparing two groups


 ✔wilcox.test(), since it doesn’t assume normality


 ✗aov(), since it’s more powerful


 ✗chisq.test(), since the normality assumption is violated






2. You want to compare a continuous variable across three or more groups, but a QQ plot shows the data is clearly non-normal in at least one group. Which function should you use?




 ✗aov()


 ✗t.test()


 ✔kruskal.test()


 ✗wilcox.test()







Solutions


When normality is clearly violated, wilcox.test() (the Wilcoxon rank-sum/Mann-Whitney test) is the appropriate choice, since it doesn’t rely on the normality assumption that t.test() requires.
kruskal.test() is the non-parametric equivalent of a one-way ANOVA, and is the appropriate choice when comparing three or more groups and the normality assumption is violated.

title: 19  Workshop 6: Statistics in R
text:
19.3 Correlation between continuous variables
So far, we have considered situations where both, or one of our variables were categorical. If both of our variables are continuous, we can measure the strength and direction of a linear relationship between them using a correlation coefficient.
A correlation coefficient ranges from -1 to 1, where:

Values close to 1 indicate a strong positive relationship (as one variable increases, so does the other)
Values close to -1 indicate a strong negative relationship (as one variable increases, the other decreases)
Values close to 0 indicate little to no linear relationship







WarningAssumptions of the Pearson correlation




The relationship between the two variables is linear (check with a scatterplot before you calculate r!)
Both variables are continuous
No extreme outliers, which can heavily distort the correlation coefficient
Ideally, both variables are roughly normally distributed

If any of these are violated (e.g. the relationship is non-linear, or there are outliers), use the non-parametric Spearman correlation instead. Spearman correlation only assumes the relationship is monotonic, since it works on the ranks of the data rather than the raw values.


Let’s examine the correlation between drug_dose_g and weight_lost_g.
First, check the linearity assumption with a scatterplot:

ggplot(dosage, aes(x = drug_dose_g, y = weight_lost_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  # add geom_smooth to compare the points to a linear
  # line of best fit
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(
    x = "Drug dose (g)",
    y = "Weight lost (g)",
    title = "Correlation between drug dose and weight lost"
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









A straight line looks like a reasonable summary of this relationship, and there don’t seem to be any crazy outliers, so let’s go ahead and calculate the correlation coefficient. We can do this in R using cor.test():

# cor.test() takes two arguments, the x and y variables
# remember these must be vectors: access from df with $
cor.test(dosage$drug_dose_g, dosage$weight_lost_g)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  dosage$drug_dose_g and dosage$weight_lost_g
t = 32.562, df = 331, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.8447622 0.8963550
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.8729789 


The correlation coefficient (0.87) is close to 1, and the p value is far smaller than 0.05, so we have strong evidence of a positive linear relationship between drug dose and weight lost. In other words, mice given a higher dose of mousezempic tended to lose more weight.






NotePearson vs Spearman correlation



cor.test() calculates a Pearson correlation by default, which as discussed above has a number of assumptions.
If your data are not normally distributed, contain outliers, or the relationship is monotonic but not linear (e.g. curved but always increasing), a Spearman correlation is a better choice. You can perform one using the method argument of cor.test():

cor.test(dosage$drug_dose_g, dosage$weight_lost_g, method = "spearman")

Warning in cor.test.default(dosage$drug_dose_g, dosage$weight_lost_g, method =
"spearman"): cannot compute exact p-value with ties



    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  dosage$drug_dose_g and dosage$weight_lost_g
S = 982284, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.8403902 










ImportantPractice exercises



Try these practice questions to test your understanding!

1. I ran the code cor.test(dosage$initial_weight_g, dosage$weight_lost_g) and got a correlation coefficient of r = 0.59, with a p value below 0.05. What can I conclude?




 ✗There is no relationship between the two variables


 ✔There is a moderate, statistically significant positive relationship between the two variables


 ✗There is a strong negative relationship between the two variables


 ✗The relationship is definitely non-linear






2. If you suspect two continuous variables have a monotonic but non-linear relationship, with a couple of outliers, which correlation method is most appropriate?




 ✗Pearson, since it’s the default in cor.test()


 ✔Spearman, since it only assumes a monotonic relationship and is more robust to outliers


 ✗Neither, correlation can’t be calculated for non-linear relationships


 ✗A linear model







Solutions


A correlation coefficient of r = 0.59 indicates a moderate positive relationship (not strong, and not negative), and since the p value is below 0.05, this relationship is statistically significant.
Spearman correlation is the better choice here, since it only assumes the relationship is monotonic (rather than strictly linear) and is calculated on the ranks of the data, making it more robust to outliers.

title: 19  Workshop 6: Statistics in R
text:
19.4 Visualising statistical tests with ggpubr
So far, we’ve been running our tests and making our plots in two separate steps. The ggpubr package (which extends ggplot2) makes it easy to combine the two, by adding the result of a statistical test directly onto a plot as an annotation. This is a great way to make quick, publication-ready figures without having to manually copy test statistics and p values into a title or label.

19.4.1 Adding a test result to a boxplot
The ggboxplot() function works similarly to ggplot() + geom_boxplot(), but returns a plot we can layer statistical annotations onto with stat_compare_means().
Let’s revisit our comparison of weight_lost_g between male and female mice, this time adding the t-test result directly onto the plot:

ggboxplot(
  data = dosage,
  # unlike in the ggplot() function, x and y are
  # supplied directly, not in aes()
  x = "sex", y = "weight_lost_g",
  # in ggpubr, you add jitter using the 'add' argument
  add = "jitter") +
  stat_compare_means(method = "t.test") +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "Weight lost (g)")








The same idea works for our three-strain comparison, using method = "kruskal.test" (or method = "anova"):

ggboxplot(dosage, x = "mouse_strain", y = "weight_lost_g", add = "jitter") +
  stat_compare_means(method = "kruskal.test") +
  labs(x = "Mouse strain", y = "Weight lost (g)")








We can get ggpubr to add pairwise comparisons too, by supplying a list of the pairs we’re interested in to the comparisons argument:

ggboxplot(dosage, x = "mouse_strain", y = "weight_lost_g", add = "jitter") +
  # get the pairwise comparisons
  stat_compare_means(
    comparisons = list(c("BALBc", "Black6"), c("BALBc", "CD1"), c("Black6", "CD1"))) +
  # get the overall p value and test name
  stat_compare_means(method = "kruskal.test", label.y = 8) +
  labs(x = "Mouse strain", y = "Weight lost (g)")

`stat_compare_means()` with `comparisons` displays *unadjusted* p-values (no correction for multiple comparisons).
ℹ For p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons, use `geom_pwc()`, or `stat_pvalue_manual()` together with `compare_means(..., p.adjust.method = )`.
This message is displayed once per session.









This runs a pairwise Wilcoxon test for each pair of strains we listed, adding a significance bracket for each comparison, alongside the overall Kruskal-Wallis result. Annoyingly, we have to run stat_compare_means() twice, because each call only adds one type of label of the plot (either the pairwise comparisons or the overall p value and test name), but this is the struggle that comes with using functions written by other people, sometimes the interface doesn’t quite make sense!


19.4.2 Adding a correlation to a scatterplot
