Similarly to ggboxplot(), ggscatter() is another higher-level plotting function from ggpubr. It creates a scatterplot that we can annotate with stat_cor() to show the correlation coefficient and p value:

ggscatter(dosage, x = "drug_dose_g", y = "weight_lost_g", add = "reg.line") +
  stat_cor(method = "pearson") +
  labs(x = "Drug dose (g)", y = "Weight lost (g)")








Just like cor.test(), we can switch to a Spearman correlation with the method argument:

ggscatter(dosage, x = "drug_dose_g", y = "weight_lost_g", add = "reg.line") +
  stat_cor(method = "spearman") +
  labs(x = "Drug dose (g)", y = "Weight lost (g)")














Noteggpubr and ggplot2



Since ggpubr functions return ordinary ggplot objects, you can keep layers to them, like theme_minimal(), labs() or even facet_wrap(). This makes ggpubr a nice shortcut for making plots, while still retaining the customisation abilities you learnt in workshop 4.








ImportantPractice exercises



Try these practice questions to test your understanding!

1. Which function would you add to a ggboxplot() to annotate it with the result of a statistical test?




 ✗stat_cor()


 ✗geom_test()


 ✔stat_compare_means()


 ✗labs()






2. I tried running the following code:

ggscatter(dosage, aes(x = "drug_dose_g", y = "weight_lost_g", add = "reg.line")) +
  stat_cor(method = "pearson")

Error:
! argument "y" is missing, with no default


But I got an error. Why?




 ✗Because you need to add the regression line with geom_smooth()


 ✔Because ggpubr plots don’t use the aes() function


 ✗Because add is not a valid ggplot2 aesthetic


 ✗Because you used the ggscatter() function instead of the ggplot() function







Solutions


stat_compare_means() adds the result of a statistical test (e.g. t-test, Kruskal-Wallis, ANOVA, or pairwise comparisons) directly onto a ggpubr plot as an annotation. stat_cor() is the equivalent for annotating a correlation coefficient onto a scatterplot.
ggscatter() is the ggpubr function for creating scatterplots, and unlike the ggplot() function it doesn’t use aes(), you just specify x and y directly to ggscatter()

title: 19  Workshop 6: Statistics in R
text:
19.5 Linear modelling (in the tidyverse)
As you may recall from lecture 4, linear models are very useful for testing for significant associations between variables, or significant differences between groups. They have the advantage of being able to correct for the effects of other variables, and thereby remove unwanted sources of variation that could otherwise reduce our ability to discover true relationships.






WarningAssumptions of linear regression




Linearity: the relationship between each predictor and the outcome is a straight line
Independence: the residuals (the differences between observed and predicted values) are independent of one another
Homoscedasticity: the residuals have roughly constant variance across the range of fitted values
Normality of residuals: the residuals are approximately normally distributed (this matters most for small samples — with a large enough sample, the model is fairly robust to this)
For multiple regression specifically: predictors shouldn’t be too strongly correlated with one another (multicollinearity)




19.5.1 Testing differences between groups (discrete x)
Earlier in this workshop (see Section 19.2.1), we used an independent t-test to check whether weight_lost_g differs between male and female mice. A simple linear regression with a single, two-level categorical predictor is mathematically identical to that t-test.
Let’s try running one, using lm() to demonstrate this. Note that just like the aov() function, we need to pipe this into summary() to get a p value:

lm(weight_lost_g ~ sex, data = dosage) %>% summary()


Call:
lm(formula = weight_lost_g ~ sex, data = dosage)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-1.2957 -0.5957 -0.2373  0.7377  1.7543 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  3.86227    0.05683  67.963  < 2e-16 ***
sexmale      0.68341    0.08001   8.542  4.9e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.73 on 331 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1806,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1781 
F-statistic: 72.96 on 1 and 331 DF,  p-value: 4.897e-16


Compare the statistic and p.value for sexmale to the t-test we ran earlier (t = -8.54, p = 4.9e-16, using var.equal = TRUE) — they match exactly. The intercept term is the mean for the reference group (female, since it comes first alphabetically), and sexmale is the estimated difference between the male and female group means.
The same is true of ANOVA: lm(y ~ group) with a 3+ level categorical predictor gives the same F-statistic and p value as aov(y ~ group).


19.5.2 Testing differences relative to 0 (discrete x)
But what if we don’t want to compare the male vs female mice, and instead are just interested in knowing whether either sex lost a meaningful amount of weight at all? This type of model could be useful, for example, if you were doing an experiment to compare a standard cancer treatment to a new drug: you might want to see how much each of these treatments affect survival relative to the baseline.
Keeping with the previous example of weight lost vs sex, if we use lm(weight_lost_g ~ 0 + sex) we get the mean weight lost per group as the estimate, and each group mean is tested against 0 rather than against the other group:

lm(weight_lost_g ~ 0 + sex, data = dosage) %>% summary()


Call:
lm(formula = weight_lost_g ~ 0 + sex, data = dosage)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-1.2957 -0.5957 -0.2373  0.7377  1.7543 

Coefficients:
          Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
sexfemale  3.86227    0.05683   67.96   <2e-16 ***
sexmale    4.54568    0.05632   80.71   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.73 on 331 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9711,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.971 
F-statistic:  5567 on 2 and 331 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Both p values are very significant (because average weight lost is nowhere near 0 g in either group). However, it is important to note that we cannot conclude from this whether male and female mice differ from each other: that comparison requires the weight_lost_g ~ sex model we used above.


19.5.3 Testing associations between variables (continuous x)
Of course, lm_test() works just as well for a continuous predictor. Earlier we used cor.test() to test the association between drug_dose_g and weight_lost_g (see the scatter plot with fitted line above), and a simple linear regression tests the same relationship, while additionally estimating a slope and intercept:

lm(weight_lost_g ~ drug_dose_g, data = dosage) %>% summary()


Call:
lm(formula = weight_lost_g ~ drug_dose_g, data = dosage)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-1.05733 -0.25979 -0.01224  0.24297  1.29389 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   -5.8721     0.3103  -18.93   <2e-16 ***
drug_dose_g 5015.3266   154.0231   32.56   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3933 on 331 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7621,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7614 
F-statistic:  1060 on 1 and 331 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The p value matches the significance we saw from cor.test(), and the (very large) slope tells us that weight lost increases steeply with drug dose. The slope is high because drug_dose_g is measured in tiny fractions of a gram, so a one-unit increase in dose is an enormous increase in practice.


19.5.4 Making linear modelling tidy
Similarly to how the tidy() function from the broom package can be used to create tidy versions of the statistical tests we’ve covered throughout this workshop, the lm_test() function from the tidyrstats package can be used to make linear modelling tidy. This is helpful if you then want to go on to do additional calculations with the results, for example to create a ggplot2 visualisation.
Another advantage is that because data is the first argument of lm_test(), we can pipe data into it:

dose_model <- dosage %>%
  lm_test(weight_lost_g ~ drug_dose_g)

Results for linear model: weight_lost_g ~ drug_dose_g

dose_model

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  term        estimate std.error statistic   p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 drug_dose_g  5015.     154.         32.6 3.13e-105
2 intercept      -5.87     0.310     -18.9 1.18e- 54


We can visualise this tidy fitted model with a scatterplot and a line of best fit:

# pull out the intercept, slope and p value from the tidy model output
model_intercept <- dose_model %>%
  filter(term == "intercept") %>%
  pull(estimate)

model_slope <- dose_model %>%
  filter(term == "drug_dose_g") %>%
  pull(estimate)

model_pvalue <- dose_model %>%
  filter(term == "drug_dose_g") %>%
  pull(p.value)

ggplot(dosage, aes(x = drug_dose_g, y = weight_lost_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  # draw the fitted line using the intercept/slope estimated by lm_test()
  geom_abline(intercept = model_intercept, slope = model_slope, colour = "blue") +
  # add the p value as a text label in the top-left corner of the plot
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = -Inf, y = Inf, # hack to put in top-left corner
    hjust = -0.1, vjust = 2,
    # format.pval is a base R function to format p values
    # in a nice human readable way
    label = paste0("p = ", format.pval(model_pvalue, digits = 3))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Drug dose (g)",
    y = "Weight lost (g)",
    title = "Relationship between drug dose and weight lost"
  )








You might be wondering why we would do this rather than simply using geom_smooth() or ggscatter(), as we have already done in this workshop. It’s important to understand that these functions fit their own model as part of the plotting, between the x and y variables on your plot. For the simple model we have just fitted between drug dosage and weight loss, it doesn’t matter, because the models made by geom_smooth() and ggscatter() are identical to the one we’ve done with lm(), but as your models become more complex, the lm_test() approach becomes necessary to visualise your actual model on a scatterplot.


19.5.5 Correcting for covariates
So far we have tested relationships between a independent (x) and a dependent (y) variable.
Often we want to ensure that other possible sources of variation are minimised so that we can better detect true differences in our ‘main effect of interest’. Say we want to understand whether drug dose affects weight lost regardless of mouse strain. In other words, we want to subtract the mean effect of any strain-specific differences.
We already saw in our ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests earlier that weight_lost_g differs noticeably between strains (Black6 mice lose more weight on average). Therefore, mouse strain is a plausible confounder of the drug dose/weight lost relationship.
To test the dose effect while correcting for strain, we can add mouse_strain to the model:

dosage %>%
  lm_test(weight_lost_g ~ drug_dose_g + mouse_strain)

Results for linear model: weight_lost_g ~ drug_dose_g + mouse_strain


# A tibble: 4 × 5
  term               estimate std.error statistic  p.value
  <chr>                 <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 drug_dose_g        4061.     308.         13.2  3.64e-32
2 intercept            -4.22     0.605      -6.98 1.68e-11
3 mouse_strainBlack6    0.490    0.0870      5.63 3.84e- 8
4 mouse_strainCD1       0.205    0.0576      3.57 4.14e- 4


The estimated slope for drug_dose_g drops from about 5015 (t ≈ 32.6) in the uncorrected model above, to about 4061 (t ≈ 13.2) once we adjust for strain — some of the raw dose/weight-lost association was indeed attributable to strain differences. Even so, the p value for drug_dose_g remains far below 0.05, so drug dose seems to have a genuine effect on weight lost that is only partly explained by strain.






ImportantPractice exercises



Try these practice questions to test your understanding. A code-based version of this exercise (investigating drug_dose_g, tail_length_mm and Simpson’s paradox) is in the practice questions at the end of the chapter, if you’d like some more hands-on practice.

1. You run lm(weight_lost_g ~ drug_dose_g, data = dosage) %>% summary() and get the following coefficients table:
Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)     0.052      0.031    1.68    0.094
drug_dose_g  5015.230    153.870   32.60   <2e-16 ***
What is the equation of the fitted regression line?




 ✔weight_lost_g = 0.052 + 5015.230 * drug_dose_g


 ✗weight_lost_g = 5015.230 + 0.052 * drug_dose_g


 ✗weight_lost_g = 32.60 * drug_dose_g


 ✗weight_lost_g = 0.094 + 5015.230 * drug_dose_g






2. Why might you want to add mouse_strain as a covariate when modelling the relationship between drug_dose_g and tail_length_mm?




 ✗To make the p value smaller


 ✔To account for mouse_strain as a potential confounder, so we can isolate the effect of drug_dose_g on its own


 ✗It’s not necessary, mouse_strain has no relationship to either variable


 ✗To calculate a correlation coefficient







Solutions


A simple linear regression follows the format y = intercept + slope * x. Here, the (Intercept) row gives us the intercept (0.052) and the drug_dose_g row gives us the slope for that predictor (5015.230), so the fitted line is weight_lost_g = 0.052 + 5015.230 * drug_dose_g. The t value and Pr(>|t|) columns are used to test whether each coefficient is significantly different from 0, not to build the equation itself.
We add mouse_strain as a covariate to account for it as a potential confounder — this lets us isolate the effect of drug_dose_g on tail_length_mm that isn’t attributable to strain differences.




Every model in this chapter has had a continuous outcome (y), such as amount of weight lost. But what if the outcome we care about is binary, for example did a mouse respond to treatment or not? In the further reading (see Section 21.2), we cover how logistic regression extends what we’ve covered here to binary outcomes.


19.5.6 The role of linear modelling in bioinformatics
Everything we’ve covered today is the basic statistical foundation for the more advanced bioinformatics techniques we’ll learn in upcoming workshops. A differential expression analysis, for example, fits exactly the same kind of linear model we’ve built today, just repeated across thousands of outcomes at once (individual genes, proteins or metabolites), while correcting for confounders like batch effects, and handling data that’s rarely as well-behaved as ours (requiring extra filtering, transformation, and care around mean-variance relationships). Doing this at scale is a computationally demanding task, which is why R packages such as limma and edgeR, bundle the expression data, sample/gene metadata and model design together into a single specialised object, then fit all of the models and generate thousands of results in one command. We’ll learn about this workflow in upcoming workshops.
Linear modelling is also foundational to machine learning, which focuses on trying to use the coefficients from a fitted model, combined with the predict() function, to make predictions about new data. We’ll explore machine learning in more detail in our final workshop.

title: 19  Workshop 6: Statistics in R
text:
19.6 Summary
Today, we’ve covered a lot of statistical ground! Here’s a quick summary of what we’ve learnt:

How to check the assumptions behind a statistical test, using QQ plots and the Shapiro-Wilk test to check normality, and a scatterplot to check linearity
How to test for an association between two categorical variables using chisq.test() (or fisher.test() for small/sparse tables)
How to compare means with a t-test (two groups) or ANOVA (three or more groups), and the assumptions (normality within groups, equal variance) that underpin them
How to choose a non-parametric alternative such as wilcox.test() or kruskal.test() when those assumptions are violated
How to calculate and visualise a correlation coefficient between two continuous variables with cor.test(), and the difference between Pearson and Spearman correlation
How to use the ggpubr package to add statistical test results directly onto a boxplot or scatterplot, for quick, publication-ready figures
How to perform a simple linear regression with both categorical and continuous predictors
How to build a multiple linear regression model to correct for confounders, and how this can reveal a true underlying relationship
Why linear modelling at the scale used in bioinformatics (e.g. differential expression analysis) requires specialised tools like the Bioconductor packages limma and edgeR

If you’d like to learn more, check out the further reading for this week, which covers logistic regression (extending everything we’ve done today to a binary outcome) along with a few other topics worth knowing about. Or check out the Learning Statistics With R ebook to cover more of the maths behind the tests we’ve learnt today.
You might also find this summary sheet helpful:
 Download the summary sheet for workshop 6 

19.6.1 Practice questions
Try these practice questions to test your understanding! Each one revisits a question we asked earlier in the chapter, but this time you’ll need to write and run the code yourself.

Were mice allocated evenly across the three experimental replicates (replicate), regardless of mouse_strain ?

Build a contingency table of mouse_strain and replicate.
Check your assumptions (i.e. expected cell counts).
Run the appropriate test and state your conclusion in plain language: is there evidence of an association between strain and replicate?
Bonus: also visualise this as a bar chart. Is your plot consistent with the result of the test?

Does a mouse’s starting weight (initial_weight_g) differ by sex? And does tail length (tail_length_mm) differ by strain? For each question, first check your assumptions, and then use an appropriate statistical test.
Do heavier mice (at the start of the study) tend to lose more weight? And is there a relationship between a mouse’s tail length and its starting weight? Visualise the relationship between the variables with a scatterplot to check the assumptions of Pearson correlation, and then perform an appropriate correlation calculation using cor.test(). Comment in words on each correlation.
Recreate your Kruskal-Wallis comparison of tail_length_mm across mouse strains (from question 2) as a ggpubr violin plot, with both the overall test result and pairwise comparisons annotated on the plot. Hint: try ggviolin() instead of ggboxplot().
Investigate whether drug_dose_g predicts tail_length_mm, and whether mouse_strain confounds that relationship. Hint: pay close attention to the sign of the slope at each step, this is a bit tricky!

Fit a linear model of drug dose (x) and tail length (y). Don’t add covariates yet. Note the direction (sign) of the slope for drug_dose_g.
Compute the mean drug_dose_g and mean tail_length_mm for each mouse_strain (hint: use the summarise() function from workshop 3). What do you notice about Black6 mice?
Now fit the linear model with mouse strain as a covariate. What happens to the sign of the drug_dose_g slope compared to step (a)? Why might correcting for a confounder actually reverse the direction of an effect, not just weaken it?




Solutions





strain_replicate_table <- table(dosage$mouse_strain, dosage$replicate)
strain_replicate_table

        
         rep1 rep2 rep3
  BALBc    26   18   24
  Black6   33   45   41
  CD1      44   50   52

chisq.test(strain_replicate_table)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  strain_replicate_table
X-squared = 3.2711, df = 4, p-value = 0.5135


Expected counts are comfortably above 5 in every cell, so the chi-squared approximation is valid. The p value (0.51) is well above 0.05, so there is no evidence of an association between strain and replicate.
For the bonus question, you can use geom_bar() as follows:

dosage %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mouse_strain, fill = replicate)) +
  # position = "fill" creates a stacked bar chart where the
  # number of mice in each replicate are depicted as a proportion
  # of the total mice for each strain. If you remove this, it
  # will just be a normal stacked bar chart where the height of
  # the bars represents count
  geom_bar(position = "fill")









Does a mouse’s starting weight (initial_weight_g) differ by sex?


# use QQ plot to check normality
ggplot(dosage, aes(sample = initial_weight_g)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~sex)







# QQ plot doesn't look great, check shapiro-wilk test
dosage %>%
  filter(sex == "male") %>%
  pull() %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.95626, p-value = 4.194e-05

dosage %>%
  filter(sex == "female") %>%
  pull() %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.95519, p-value = 3.925e-05

# both p < 0.05: normality assumption is violated
# need to use non-parametric test (wilcox)
wilcox.test(initial_weight_g ~ sex, data = dosage)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  initial_weight_g by sex
W = 8178, p-value = 9.901e-11
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


initial_weight_g is non-normal in both groups (Shapiro-Wilk p value < 0.001), so a Wilcoxon test is the best choice. It shows a statistically significant difference: males are heavier.
Does tail length (tail_length_mm) differ by strain?

# use QQ plot to check normality
ggplot(dosage, aes(sample = tail_length_mm)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~mouse_strain)







# QQ plot looks so-so, check shapiro-wilk test
dosage %>%
  filter(mouse_strain == "Black6") %>%
  pull() %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.95692, p-value = 0.0007659

dosage %>%
  filter(mouse_strain == "CD1") %>%
  pull() %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.95872, p-value = 0.0002326

dosage %>%
  filter(mouse_strain == "BALBc") %>%
  pull() %>%
  shapiro.test()


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  .
W = 0.95505, p-value = 0.01544

# all <0.05, normality is violated. use kruskal wallace test
kruskal.test(tail_length_mm ~ mouse_strain, data = dosage)


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  tail_length_mm by mouse_strain
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 217.56, df = 2, p-value < 2.2e-16


Tail length is non-normal, so the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test should be used. There is a statistically significant difference (Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.001) in tail length between mouse strains.

Do heavier mice (at the start of the study) tend to lose more weight?


ggplot(dosage, aes(x = initial_weight_g, y = weight_lost_g)) +
  geom_point()







cor.test(dosage$initial_weight_g, dosage$weight_lost_g)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  dosage$initial_weight_g and dosage$weight_lost_g
t = 13.276, df = 331, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.5145745 0.6554058
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.5894511 


initial_weight_g and weight_lost_g are moderately positively correlated (r ≈ 0.59, p < 0.001), so heavier mice tended to lose more weight.
Is there a relationship between a mouse’s tail length and its starting weight?

ggplot(dosage, aes(x = tail_length_mm, y = initial_weight_g)) +
  geom_point()







cor.test(dosage$tail_length_mm, dosage$initial_weight_g)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  dosage$tail_length_mm and dosage$initial_weight_g
t = -4.2726, df = 331, p-value = 2.528e-05
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.3280409 -0.1242017
sample estimates:
       cor 
-0.2286256 


tail_length_mm and initial_weight_g are weakly negatively correlated (r ≈ -0.23, p < 0.001), so mice with longer tails tend to weigh more.




ggviolin(dosage, x = "mouse_strain", y = "tail_length_mm", add = "jitter") +
  stat_compare_means(
    comparisons = list(c("BALBc", "Black6"), c("BALBc", "CD1"), c("Black6", "CD1"))) +
  # get the overall p value and test name
  stat_compare_means(method = "kruskal.test", label.y = 9) +
  labs(x = "Mouse strain", y = "Tail length (mm)")












dosage %>% lm_test(tail_length_mm ~ drug_dose_g)

Results for linear model: tail_length_mm ~ drug_dose_g


# A tibble: 2 × 5
  term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 intercept       33.5      1.27      26.4 2.51e-83
2 drug_dose_g  -8118.     630.       -12.9 4.78e-31


The slope is -8188 indicating as drug dose increases, tail length decreases.

dosage %>% summarise(
  mean_dose = mean(drug_dose_g),
  mean_tail_len = mean(tail_length_mm),
  .by = mouse_strain)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  mouse_strain mean_dose mean_tail_len
  <chr>            <dbl>         <dbl>
1 CD1            0.00190          18.3
2 Black6         0.00217          15.0
3 BALBc          0.00196          18.4


We notice that Black-6 mice have (on average) higher drug dosages and shorter tails.

dosage %>% lm_test(tail_length_mm ~ drug_dose_g + mouse_strain)

Results for linear model: tail_length_mm ~ drug_dose_g + mouse_strain


# A tibble: 4 × 5
  term               estimate std.error statistic  p.value
  <chr>                 <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 mouse_strainBlack6   -5.20      0.228    -22.8  1.42e-69
2 drug_dose_g        8288.      808.        10.3  1.36e-21
3 mouse_strainCD1       0.401     0.151      2.65 8.37e- 3
4 intercept             2.19      1.59       1.38 1.68e- 1


We can now see that the slope is 8288: it has changed sign from negative to positive.
This is a good example of Simpson’s paradox: the uncorrected slope for drug_dose_g is strongly negative (higher dose associated with shorter tails), but Black6 mice happen to have both a higher average dose and much shorter tails than the other strains. Once mouse_strain is added to the model, the drug_dose_g slope flips to strongly positive. That is, within any given strain, higher doses are actually associated with longer tails. The uncorrected relationship was driven entirely by strain differences, not a true dose effect in the opposite direction. We saw a similar flip in workshop 4, when adding colour to a scatterplot changed our interpretation of the relationship between initial weight and tail length (see Chapter 13).

title: 20  Tutorial 8: Working with strings in R
text:
20.1 Introducing today’s data
So far in this subject, we’ve only worked with relatively short string (character) data, like the mouse_strain variable from the dosage dataset. Today, we’ll work with longer, more complex strings and learn about a useful tidyverse package, stringr, that helps us to do this. These skills are very useful for cleaning up messy spreadsheet entries, or pull structured information out of free-text notes.
Like last week’s git tutorial, this is designed to be mostly self-paced: work through it independently or with friends, running the code as you go and having a go at the extra activities. We will be here to help, and can go through the trickier bits together as a class, so don’t worry if something doesn’t click on the first attempt.
Let’s imagine that the mousezempic experiements went really well, and the drug (which has been creatively renamed Humanzempic for human use) has now progressed to a small Phase 1 human trial across two hospital sites: the Royal Melbourne Hospital (RMH) and Western Health (WH). As part of this trial, doctors have been recording basic patient information along with some free-text clinical notes.
As always, let’s start by loading the packages and reading in the data. Today, we’ll read in data directly from the web, by supplying the URL to the read_csv() function instead of a local file path on your computer:
library(tidyverse)
patients <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WEHI-Education/BIOL90042_R_Course/refs/heads/main/data/patient_data.csv")
Let’s start by taking a look at the patients dataframe:
patients

# A tibble: 13 × 8
   site  patient_num first_name last_name    age blood_pressure symptoms        
   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <dbl> <chr>          <chr>           
 1 RMH             1 Amara      Osei          54 132/85         nausea, fatigue 
 2 RMH             2 Liam       Fitzgerald    61 145/92         headache, dizzi…
 3 WH              1 Priya      Nair          47 118/76         fatigue         
 4 WH              2 Noah       Kim           39 122/80         nausea, vomiting
 5 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson      58 150/95         chest pain, sho…
 6 WH              3 Ethan      Walsh         44 128/82         fatigue, headac…
 7 RMH             4 Zara       Ibrahim       29 110/70         nausea          
 8 WH              4 Oliver     Ngata         63 140/88         fatigue, nausea 
 9 RMH             5 Isla       MacDonald     51 135/86         headache        
10 WH              5 Kai        Tupou         36 120/78         fever, cough    
11 RMH             6 Sofia      Marchetti     49 126/81         nausea, fatigue 
12 WH              6 Mateo      Silva         41 130/84         dizziness       
13 RMH             7 Ana        Petrovic      55 129/83         fatigue         
# ℹ 1 more variable: clinical_notes <chr>
There are 8 columns:
This data violates several of the rules of tidy data we learnt in Chapter 10, as many pieces of information are crammed into single columns (e.g. the blood_pressure column or symptoms columns), making it difficult to perform analysis.

title: 20  Tutorial 8: Working with strings in R
text:
20.2 Part 1: string basics
First, let’s work on cleaning up the patients data a little. We will use some of what we already know about data wrangling, while learning new things we can do with this string data.

20.2.1 Combining strings with paste() and paste0()
Usually, when working with patient data, it should be anonymised, so we should use a unique patient ID rather than first and last names. Let’s begin by creating a new column in patients with a patient ID, that is created by combining the site and patient_num columns (so RMH-1, RMH-2, etc)
We can do this using the paste() or paste0() functions, which allow us to stick strings together. For example, let’s say I wanted to combine the strings "Hello" and "world":
paste() combines its arguments into one string, with a space between each one by default:

paste("Hello", "world")

[1] "Hello world"


You can change the separator using the sep argument:

paste("Hello", "world", sep = "_")

[1] "Hello_world"


paste0() is a shortcut for paste(..., sep = ""), so it joins strings with nothing in between:

paste0("Hello", "world")

[1] "Helloworld"


So, if we wanted to combine the site and patient_num, with a dash in-between we could run:

# using paste
paste(patients$site, patients$patient_num, sep = "-")

 [1] "RMH-1" "RMH-2" "WH-1"  "WH-2"  "RMH-3" "WH-3"  "RMH-4" "WH-4"  "RMH-5"
[10] "WH-5"  "RMH-6" "WH-6"  "RMH-7"

# using paste0
paste0(patients$site, "-", patients$patient_num)

 [1] "RMH-1" "RMH-2" "WH-1"  "WH-2"  "RMH-3" "WH-3"  "RMH-4" "WH-4"  "RMH-5"
[10] "WH-5"  "RMH-6" "WH-6"  "RMH-7"


We can apply this knowledge to create a patient_id column using mutate(), and then remove the first and last name columns to protect the patients privacy:

patients_anon <- patients %>%
  # use mutate to create
  mutate(patient_id = paste0(site, "-", patient_num)) %>%
  # use select with - sign to remove columns
  select(-first_name, -last_name)







ImportantPractice activity: creating patient summary strings



Although we want anonymised data for our analysis, the billing department needs the full names, ages and ID of the patients for their records.
Use paste0() to create a new column called patient_summary that has the form "Amara Osei (54), RMH-1" (i.e. the patient’s full name, their age in brackets, and their patient ID).


Solution


patients %>%
  mutate(
    patient_summary = paste0(
      first_name, " ", last_name,  " (", age, "), ", site, "-", patient_num)) %>%
  select(patient_summary)

# A tibble: 13 × 1
   patient_summary            
   <chr>                      
 1 Amara Osei (54), RMH-1     
 2 Liam Fitzgerald (61), RMH-2
 3 Priya Nair (47), WH-1      
 4 Noah Kim (39), WH-2        
 5 Grace Thompson (58), RMH-3 
 6 Ethan Walsh (44), WH-3     
 7 Zara Ibrahim (29), RMH-4   
 8 Oliver Ngata (63), WH-4    
 9 Isla MacDonald (51), RMH-5 
10 Kai Tupou (36), WH-5       
11 Sofia Marchetti (49), RMH-6
12 Mateo Silva (41), WH-6     
13 Ana Petrovic (55), RMH-7   







20.2.2 Counting characters
Next, the trial coordindator has asked us to flag any clinical notes that seem too short– apparently some of the doctors have been slacking off lately!
We can do this using the nchar() function, which counts the number of characters in a string:

nchar("Humanzempic")

[1] 11








ImportantPractice activity: flagging brief notes



Use nchar() and filter() to find any patients whose clinical_notes are shorter than 30 characters.


Solution


patients %>%
  filter(nchar(clinical_notes) < 30)

# A tibble: 1 × 8
  site  patient_num first_name last_name   age blood_pressure symptoms
  <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     <dbl> <chr>          <chr>   
1 RMH             7 Ana        Petrovic     55 129/83         fatigue 
# ℹ 1 more variable: clinical_notes <chr>


There is just one: patient RMH-7 (Ana Petrovic) has clinical notes that just say "Dr. Lee: Stable.". This doctor might need following up with!





20.2.3 Reshaping data using string columns
Back in workshop 3, we learnt about the separate() function from the tidyr package, and used it to split up a single character column of the form gene_replicate into separate gene and replicate columns (see Section 10.6.2). Let’s revisit this concept now, using the separate_longer_delim() and separate_wider_delim() functions, which give us control over whether to split a string into more rows (longer), or more columns (wider).

20.2.3.1 Getting one symptom per row with separate_longer_delim()
Some patients have multiple symptoms, stored as a single comma-separated string, e.g "nausea, fatigue". This isn’t very tidy: if we want to count how common each symptom is, we first need one row per symptom, rather than one row per patient.
This is what the separate_longer_delim() function does: it takes the name of a column and a delimiter, and creates a new row each time it finds that delimiter:

patients %>%
  separate_longer_delim(symptoms, delim = ", ")

# A tibble: 21 × 8
   site  patient_num first_name last_name    age blood_pressure symptoms        
   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <dbl> <chr>          <chr>           
 1 RMH             1 Amara      Osei          54 132/85         nausea          
 2 RMH             1 Amara      Osei          54 132/85         fatigue         
 3 RMH             2 Liam       Fitzgerald    61 145/92         headache        
 4 RMH             2 Liam       Fitzgerald    61 145/92         dizziness       
 5 WH              1 Priya      Nair          47 118/76         fatigue         
 6 WH              2 Noah       Kim           39 122/80         nausea          
 7 WH              2 Noah       Kim           39 122/80         vomiting        
 8 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson      58 150/95         chest pain      
 9 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson      58 150/95         shortness of br…
10 WH              3 Ethan      Walsh         44 128/82         fatigue         
# ℹ 11 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: clinical_notes <chr>


Remember that a delimeter just means a character used to separate things, in this case a comma, but it can be any character, often a dash, space or underscore.
Now that we have one symptom per row, we can use the count() function to see which symptoms are most common in the trial:

patients %>%
  separate_longer_delim(symptoms, delim = ", ") %>%
  count(symptoms, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 9 × 2
  symptoms                n
  <chr>               <int>
1 fatigue                 6
2 nausea                  5
3 headache                3
4 dizziness               2
5 chest pain              1
6 cough                   1
7 fever                   1
8 shortness of breath     1
9 vomiting                1








ImportantPractice activity: visualising symptom frequency



Using the long-form data you made above, produce a bar chart showing how many patients reported each symptom, using ggplot2’s geom_bar().


Solution


patients %>%
  separate_longer_delim(symptoms, delim = ", ") %>%
  # using fct_infreq() automatically converts symptoms to
  # a factor, and orders it by frequency
  ggplot(aes(y = fct_infreq(symptoms))) +
    geom_bar() +
    theme_classic() +
    labs(
      x = "Symptom", y = "Number of patients",
      title = "Frequency of reported symptoms")













20.2.3.2 Splitting blood pressure into two columns with separate_wider_delim()
Unlike the symptoms column, the blood_pressure contains two separate pieces of information (systolic and diastolic blood pressure) that we’d like as their own columns, rather than as extra rows.
We can do this using separate_wider_delim(), which takes in addition to the column you want to separate and the delimiter, also a vector of names for the new columns, like so:

patients %>%
  separate_wider_delim(
    blood_pressure,
    delim = "/",
    names = c("systolic", "diastolic")
  )

# A tibble: 13 × 9
   site  patient_num first_name last_name    age systolic diastolic symptoms    
   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <dbl> <chr>    <chr>     <chr>       
 1 RMH             1 Amara      Osei          54 132      85        nausea, fat…
 2 RMH             2 Liam       Fitzgerald    61 145      92        headache, d…
 3 WH              1 Priya      Nair          47 118      76        fatigue     
 4 WH              2 Noah       Kim           39 122      80        nausea, vom…
 5 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson      58 150      95        chest pain,…
 6 WH              3 Ethan      Walsh         44 128      82        fatigue, he…
 7 RMH             4 Zara       Ibrahim       29 110      70        nausea      
 8 WH              4 Oliver     Ngata         63 140      88        fatigue, na…
 9 RMH             5 Isla       MacDonald     51 135      86        headache    
10 WH              5 Kai        Tupou         36 120      78        fever, cough
11 RMH             6 Sofia      Marchetti     49 126      81        nausea, fat…
12 WH              6 Mateo      Silva         41 130      84        dizziness   
13 RMH             7 Ana        Petrovic      55 129      83        fatigue     
# ℹ 1 more variable: clinical_notes <chr>








ImportantPractice activity: analysing blood pressure



Now that the systolic and diastolic blood pressures are in their own columns, we can convert them to numeric and perform some analysis of them (e.g. calculating summary statistics).
Find the mean of both systolic and diastolic blood pressure.


Solution


# first let's save our separated data as its own variable
patients_bp_sep <- patients %>%
  separate_wider_delim(
    blood_pressure,
    delim = "/",
    names = c("systolic", "diastolic")
  )

# now, calculate summary stats for each:
patients_bp_sep %>% 
  # get systolic column
  pull(systolic) %>%
  # convert to numeric first 
  as.numeric() %>%
  summary()

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  110.0   122.0   129.0   129.6   135.0   150.0 

# repeat same for diastolic
patients_bp_sep %>% 
  pull(diastolic) %>%
  as.numeric() %>%
  summary()

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  70.00   80.00   83.00   83.08   86.00   95.00

title: 20  Tutorial 8: Working with strings in R
text:
20.3 Part 2: using stringr and regex
For the rest of today’s session, we’ll be using functions from the stringr package (loaded automatically as part of the tidyverse) to search for, extract and replace text.
Most stringr functions take the same first two arguments:

string, which is the string you want to run the function on. This can be a single string like "cats" or a character vector.
pattern, which is the pattern you want to find/replace/extract etc. This is often, but not always, a regular expression.

Note that because stringr functions work on vectors, to use them on columns in a data frame, you need to either use dataframe$column syntax, or use them within dplyr functions like filter() or mutate().

20.3.1 Regular expressions
Regular expressions (usually shortened to ‘regex’) are an extremely powerful (and complex!) language for describing patterns within strings. Have you ever created a new password for a website, and been told it isn’t long enough, or doesn’t contain a special character? These checks are handled by regex, and in data analysis you can use them to filter your data, or extract numbers from blocks of text.
Regex is extremely complicated, and we could probably spend a whole semester on it alone. This quote sums it up nicely:

Some people, when confronted with a problem, think “I know, I’ll use regular expressions.” Now they have two problems.
—Jamie Zawinski

For today, let’s just consider the following:







Pattern
Matches




"fever"
The exact text fever (a fixed pattern)


\\d
Any single digit (0–9)


\\w
Any letter or number


.
Any single character


*
0 or more matches (e.g. x* matches '' or 'x' or 'xx' and so on)


+
1 or more matches (e.g. x* matches 'x' or 'xx' and so on. Doesn’t match empty string)


^
The start of the string


$
The end of the string


\\.
A literal full stop (since . alone means ‘any character’, we need to ‘escape’ it with \\)



Don’t worry if it doesn’t make sense yet! We’ll see some examples below, and regex is very much a ‘learn by doing’ skill so it will just take time. It’s also completely fine to ask AI for help writing a tricky regex pattern, so long as you check and understand what it’s doing before you use it!


20.3.2 Detecting patterns with str_detect()
str_detect(string, pattern) checks whether a pattern is found anywhere inside each string, and returns TRUE or FALSE:

str_detect("Patient reports mild fever", "fever")

[1] TRUE


Because it returns a logical value, str_detect() is extremely useful combined with filter(), to keep only the rows of a data frame where a pattern is present. For example, let’s find every patient whose clinical notes mention "fatigue":

patients %>%
  filter(str_detect(clinical_notes, "fatigue"))

# A tibble: 5 × 8
  site  patient_num first_name last_name   age blood_pressure symptoms         
  <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     <dbl> <chr>          <chr>            
1 RMH             1 Amara      Osei         54 132/85         nausea, fatigue  
2 WH              1 Priya      Nair         47 118/76         fatigue          
3 WH              3 Ethan      Walsh        44 128/82         fatigue, headache
4 WH              4 Oliver     Ngata        63 140/88         fatigue, nausea  
5 RMH             6 Sofia      Marchetti    49 126/81         nausea, fatigue  
# ℹ 1 more variable: clinical_notes <chr>








ImportantPractice activity: finding a possible adverse event



The trial coordinators are concerned about Grace Thompson’s case, and want to check whether any other patients have reported similar cardiac symptoms. Use str_detect() and filter() to find any patients whose clinical_notes mention "chest pain" and see whether this is something multiple people have experienced.


Solution


patients %>%
  filter(str_detect(clinical_notes, "chest pain"))

# A tibble: 1 × 8
  site  patient_num first_name last_name   age blood_pressure symptoms          
  <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     <dbl> <chr>          <chr>             
1 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson     58 150/95         chest pain, short…
# ℹ 1 more variable: clinical_notes <chr>


Only Grace Thompson (RMH-3) mentions chest pain in this dataset, which is reassuring.





20.3.3 Subsetting a character vector with str_subset()
str_detect() tells you whether each string matches, but sometimes you just want the matching strings themselves, without having to use filter.
str_subset(string, pattern) returns the values of string that contained pattern, but it only works on a character vector, not directly on a whole data frame.

str_subset(patients$clinical_notes, "chest pain")

[1] "Dr. Ahmed: Patient reports chest pain and shortness of breath. Humanzempic dose withheld pending cardiology review."








ImportantPractice activity: mild symptoms



Imagine we are interested in patients experiencing ‘mild’ symptoms Use str_subset() to find all mentions of mild symptoms in the clinical_notes column.


Solution


str_subset(patients$clinical_notes, "mild")

[1] "Dr. Chen: Patient reports mild nausea and fatigue since starting 500mg Humanzempic three weeks ago. Advised to take medication with food. Follow-up in 4 weeks."
[2] "Dr. Singh: Ongoing fatigue and mild nausea on 500mg Humanzempic. Patient otherwise stable."                                                                     
[3] "Dr. Singh: Patient reports mild dizziness, blood pressure stable. Continuing 500mg Humanzempic."                                                                







20.3.4 Extracting parts of a string that match a pattern with str_extract()
So far, we’ve learnt how to find patterns in our strings, but what if we want to extract just the parts of the string that match that pattern? This is where regular expressions start to become really powerful, when combined with str_extract(string, pattern) which returns the part of the string that matches the pattern (or NA if there’s no match).
For example, most of the clinical notes mention the Humanzempic dose, written as a number of digits followed directly by "mg". We can extract the dose using the regex pattern "\\d+mg" (one or more digits, followed by "mg"):

patients %>%
  mutate(dose = str_extract(clinical_notes, "\\d+mg"))

# A tibble: 13 × 9
   site  patient_num first_name last_name    age blood_pressure symptoms        
   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <dbl> <chr>          <chr>           
 1 RMH             1 Amara      Osei          54 132/85         nausea, fatigue 
 2 RMH             2 Liam       Fitzgerald    61 145/92         headache, dizzi…
 3 WH              1 Priya      Nair          47 118/76         fatigue         
 4 WH              2 Noah       Kim           39 122/80         nausea, vomiting
 5 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson      58 150/95         chest pain, sho…
 6 WH              3 Ethan      Walsh         44 128/82         fatigue, headac…
 7 RMH             4 Zara       Ibrahim       29 110/70         nausea          
 8 WH              4 Oliver     Ngata         63 140/88         fatigue, nausea 
 9 RMH             5 Isla       MacDonald     51 135/86         headache        
10 WH              5 Kai        Tupou         36 120/78         fever, cough    
11 RMH             6 Sofia      Marchetti     49 126/81         nausea, fatigue 
12 WH              6 Mateo      Silva         41 130/84         dizziness       
13 RMH             7 Ana        Petrovic      55 129/83         fatigue         
# ℹ 2 more variables: clinical_notes <chr>, dose <chr>








NoteHow many matches?



It’s always good practice to check that your regex is working as intended. If you view the patients dataframe, you might notice that Noah Kim (patient ID: WH-2) was originally taking 1000mg, but the doctor has dropped the dose to 500mg. However, our dose column only contains the old dose, 1000mg.
This is because the stringr functions find the first match, not all matches. Many of the functions, including str_extract() have a variant ending in _all that allow you to find all matches, like str_extract_all().








ImportantPractice activity: extracting the treating doctor



Every clinical note begins with the treating doctor’s surname, written in the format "Dr. Surname:" (for example, "Dr. Chen:").
Use str_extract() with the regex pattern "Dr\\. \\w+" to create a new column called doctor containing just this part of the note.
(Pattern explanation: \\w matches any single ‘word’ character, i.e. a letter, digit or underscore, and \\. matches a literal full stop.)


Solution


patients %>%
  mutate(doctor = str_extract(clinical_notes, "Dr\\. \\w+"))

# A tibble: 13 × 9
   site  patient_num first_name last_name    age blood_pressure symptoms        
   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <dbl> <chr>          <chr>           
 1 RMH             1 Amara      Osei          54 132/85         nausea, fatigue 
 2 RMH             2 Liam       Fitzgerald    61 145/92         headache, dizzi…
 3 WH              1 Priya      Nair          47 118/76         fatigue         
 4 WH              2 Noah       Kim           39 122/80         nausea, vomiting
 5 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson      58 150/95         chest pain, sho…
 6 WH              3 Ethan      Walsh         44 128/82         fatigue, headac…
 7 RMH             4 Zara       Ibrahim       29 110/70         nausea          
 8 WH              4 Oliver     Ngata         63 140/88         fatigue, nausea 
 9 RMH             5 Isla       MacDonald     51 135/86         headache        
10 WH              5 Kai        Tupou         36 120/78         fever, cough    
11 RMH             6 Sofia      Marchetti     49 126/81         nausea, fatigue 
12 WH              6 Mateo      Silva         41 130/84         dizziness       
13 RMH             7 Ana        Petrovic      55 129/83         fatigue         
# ℹ 2 more variables: clinical_notes <chr>, doctor <chr>







20.3.5 Editing strings with str_remove() and str_replace()
We often want to clean up messy text by removing or swapping out matched patterns entirely. str_remove(string, pattern) deletes the first match of pattern from each string, and str_replace(string, pattern, replacement) swaps it out for some new text instead.
Let’s use str_remove() to strip the "Dr. Surname: " prefix off the front of each note, so we’re left with just the clinical content:

patients %>%
  mutate(clinical_notes = str_remove(clinical_notes, "^Dr\\. \\w+: "))

# A tibble: 13 × 8
   site  patient_num first_name last_name    age blood_pressure symptoms        
   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <dbl> <chr>          <chr>           
 1 RMH             1 Amara      Osei          54 132/85         nausea, fatigue 
 2 RMH             2 Liam       Fitzgerald    61 145/92         headache, dizzi…
 3 WH              1 Priya      Nair          47 118/76         fatigue         
 4 WH              2 Noah       Kim           39 122/80         nausea, vomiting
 5 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson      58 150/95         chest pain, sho…
 6 WH              3 Ethan      Walsh         44 128/82         fatigue, headac…
 7 RMH             4 Zara       Ibrahim       29 110/70         nausea          
 8 WH              4 Oliver     Ngata         63 140/88         fatigue, nausea 
 9 RMH             5 Isla       MacDonald     51 135/86         headache        
10 WH              5 Kai        Tupou         36 120/78         fever, cough    
11 RMH             6 Sofia      Marchetti     49 126/81         nausea, fatigue 
12 WH              6 Mateo      Silva         41 130/84         dizziness       
13 RMH             7 Ana        Petrovic      55 129/83         fatigue         
# ℹ 1 more variable: clinical_notes <chr>


Notice the ^ at the start of the pattern. This ‘anchors’ the match to the beginning of the string, so we only remove the doctor’s name if it appears right at the start (rather than accidentally matching a doctor’s name mentioned anywhere else in the note).
We could use str_replace() if, say, the trial had to be blinded and every mention of the drug name needed to be swapped out for a neutral placeholder:

patients %>%
  mutate(clinical_notes = str_replace(clinical_notes, "Humanzempic", "the study drug"))

# A tibble: 13 × 8
   site  patient_num first_name last_name    age blood_pressure symptoms        
   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <dbl> <chr>          <chr>           
 1 RMH             1 Amara      Osei          54 132/85         nausea, fatigue 
 2 RMH             2 Liam       Fitzgerald    61 145/92         headache, dizzi…
 3 WH              1 Priya      Nair          47 118/76         fatigue         
 4 WH              2 Noah       Kim           39 122/80         nausea, vomiting
 5 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson      58 150/95         chest pain, sho…
 6 WH              3 Ethan      Walsh         44 128/82         fatigue, headac…
 7 RMH             4 Zara       Ibrahim       29 110/70         nausea          
 8 WH              4 Oliver     Ngata         63 140/88         fatigue, nausea 
 9 RMH             5 Isla       MacDonald     51 135/86         headache        
10 WH              5 Kai        Tupou         36 120/78         fever, cough    
11 RMH             6 Sofia      Marchetti     49 126/81         nausea, fatigue 
12 WH              6 Mateo      Silva         41 130/84         dizziness       
13 RMH             7 Ana        Petrovic      55 129/83         fatigue         
# ℹ 1 more variable: clinical_notes <chr>








Notestr_remove() vs str_replace()



str_remove(string, pattern) is actually a shortcut for str_replace(string, pattern, ""), because removing is just replacing with nothing! Keep in mind that both functions only act on the first match in each string. If you want to replace every match, use str_remove_all() or str_replace_all() instead.








ImportantPractice activity: de-identifying dosage information



For privacy reasons, the trial coordinators want a fully de-identified copy of the notes that hides the exact dosage. Use str_replace_all() to replace every digit in each patient’s clinical_notes with the letter "X" (so "500mg" becomes "XXXmg").
(Hint: remember that \\d matches a single digit, and you’ll want to replace every match, not just the first one.)


Solution


patients %>%
  mutate(clinical_notes = str_replace_all(clinical_notes, "\\d", "X"))

# A tibble: 13 × 8
   site  patient_num first_name last_name    age blood_pressure symptoms        
   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <dbl> <chr>          <chr>           
 1 RMH             1 Amara      Osei          54 132/85         nausea, fatigue 
 2 RMH             2 Liam       Fitzgerald    61 145/92         headache, dizzi…
 3 WH              1 Priya      Nair          47 118/76         fatigue         
 4 WH              2 Noah       Kim           39 122/80         nausea, vomiting
 5 RMH             3 Grace      Thompson      58 150/95         chest pain, sho…
 6 WH              3 Ethan      Walsh         44 128/82         fatigue, headac…
 7 RMH             4 Zara       Ibrahim       29 110/70         nausea          
 8 WH              4 Oliver     Ngata         63 140/88         fatigue, nausea 
 9 RMH             5 Isla       MacDonald     51 135/86         headache        
10 WH              5 Kai        Tupou         36 120/78         fever, cough    
11 RMH             6 Sofia      Marchetti     49 126/81         nausea, fatigue 
12 WH              6 Mateo      Silva         41 130/84         dizziness       
13 RMH             7 Ana        Petrovic      55 129/83         fatigue         
# ℹ 1 more variable: clinical_notes <chr>

title: 20  Tutorial 8: Working with strings in R
text:
20.4 Putting it all together
Let’s finish with one activity that combines several of today’s functions.






ImportantPractice activity: a tidy summary table



Starting from the original patients data frame, write code that:

Extracts the Humanzempic dose from clinical_notes into a new column called dose
Filters the data to keep only patients whose clinical notes mention "nausea"
Removes the units in the dose column, and converts it to numeric
Calculates the mean dosage of patients experiencing nausea



Solution


patients %>%
  # extract the dose
  mutate(
    dose = str_extract(clinical_notes, "\\d+mg")
  ) %>%
  # filter to just patients with nausea
  filter(str_detect(clinical_notes, "nausea")) %>%
  # remove mg and convert dose to numeric
  mutate(dose = as.numeric(str_remove(dose, "mg"))) %>%
  # calculate the mean dose
  pull(dose) %>%
  mean()

[1] 583.3333

20.5 Further resources for working with strings
Today we’ve learnt the basics of stringr and regex, but there is a lot more to strings! If you’d like to go further, these are some good resources:

The stringr cheatsheet summarises the different functions in the stringr package, as well as some common regex patterns
Chapter 15 of R for Data Science covers strings and regular expressions in much greater depth
Regex101 is a handy website that allows you to try out regex in your browser
The stringdist R package, which allows you to do ‘fuzzy’ (non-exact) matching, to tolerate typos

title: 21  Further Reading
text:
21.1 Calculating correlations between all pairs of continuous variables
In this week’s further reading, we will cover various interesting topics that didn’t make it into workshop 6.
We will use same packages and data as for workshop 6:
In workshop 6, we learnt how to calculate a correlation coefficient for a pair of continuous variables (see Section 19.3). But what if we aren’t sure which pair of continuous variables we’re interested in? We can examine the correlation between every pair of continuous variables at once, and visualise the resulting correlation matrix as a heatmap using the ggcorrplot package.
First, we need to install and load ggcorrplot:
install.packages("ggcorrplot")
library(ggcorrplot)
Then, we can use it as follows:
dosage %>%
  # first select the columns of interest
  # these columns should be numeric
  select(drug_dose_g, weight_lost_g, tail_length_mm, initial_weight_g) %>%
  # use cor() to calculate the pairwise correlation between these
  cor() %>%
  # visualise the correlation using ggcorrplot
  ggcorrplot(
    # default is lab = FALSE,
    # lab = TRUE adds the correlation coefficient to the plot
    lab = TRUE,
    title = "Correlation matrix of continuous variables"
  )
This gives us a great overview of all the numeric variables in our dataset!

title: 21  Further Reading
text:
21.2 Logistic regression
Every model we fitted in workshop 6 had a continuous outcome (y), such as weight lost. But often in biology the outcome we care about is binary:

Did a patient respond to treatment or not?
Did a tumour recur or not?
Did a mouse survive or not?

A straight line is a poor model for a binary outcome, because it can predict probabilities below 0 or above 1. Logistic regression solves this by modelling the log-odds of the outcome as a linear function of the predictors:
\[
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_1 + \hat\beta_2 x_2 + \dots
\]
where \(p\) is the probability of the outcome occurring. This keeps the right-hand side of the equation looking just like a linear model, while guaranteeing that the predicted probability \(p\) stays between 0 and 1.






WarningAssumptions of logistic regression




Each continuous predictor is linearly related to the log-odds of the outcome (not to the raw probability)
Independence of observations
No perfect separation: no combination of predictors perfectly predicts the outcome (this makes the model unstable)
A reasonably large sample size relative to the number of predictors, and ideally a good number of events in the rarer outcome category

Note that, unlike linear regression, logistic regression does not assume normally distributed or homoscedastic residuals, since the outcome is binary rather than continuous



21.2.1 Create a binary outcome
The mousezempic dosage data doesn’t come with a binary outcome built in, so let’s create one: we’ll define a mouse as a “responder” (1) if it lost more weight than the median mouse in the study, and a “non-responder” (0) otherwise.
We’ll also rescale drug_dose_g (originally measured in tiny fractions of a gram) into a standardised z-score, so that the resulting odds ratio has a sensible interpretation (“per 1 standard deviation increase in dose”) rather than an astronomically large number per 1 g increase.

dosage <- dosage %>%
  na.omit(weight_lost_g, drug_dose_g) %>%
  mutate(
    responder = case_when(
      weight_lost_g > median(weight_lost_g) ~ 1,
      weight_lost_g < median(weight_lost_g) ~ 0,
      .default = NA),
    drug_dose_z = as.numeric(scale(drug_dose_g))
  )

dosage %>% count(responder)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  responder     n
      <dbl> <int>
1         0   166
2         1   161
3        NA     6




21.2.2 Check for separation
Before fitting the model, we should check for separation, where a predictor perfectly separates responders from non-responders, which would make the model unstable. A quick contingency table is one way to check this by eye:

table(dosage$mouse_strain, dosage$responder)

        
           0   1
  BALBc   53  11
  Black6   1 118
  CD1    112  32


Every strain contains a mix of responders and non-responders, so separation isn’t a concern here.


21.2.3 Fit the logistic regression model
Does drug dose predict the probability of responding, after accounting for mouse strain? Use logistic regression to find out, with the glm() function:

# save as variable so we can do more with it later
logit_model <- glm(
  responder ~ drug_dose_z + mouse_strain,
  data = dosage,
  family = "binomial"
)

summary(logit_model)


Call:
glm(formula = responder ~ drug_dose_z + mouse_strain, family = "binomial", 
    data = dosage)

Coefficients:
                   Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)         -1.0148     0.3787  -2.679  0.00737 ** 
drug_dose_z          2.6850     0.4928   5.449 5.08e-08 ***
mouse_strainBlack6   3.3002     1.1513   2.866  0.00415 ** 
mouse_strainCD1      1.5186     0.4999   3.038  0.00238 ** 
---

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

21.2.4 Interpret coefficients as odds ratios
The raw coefficients from summary() are on the log-odds scale, which isn’t very intuitive. We can make them easier to interpret by exponentiating them. ‘Exponentiating’ converts each coefficient into an odds ratio (OR), which is how much the odds of responding multiply for each one-unit increase in that predictor (holding other predictors constant). The easiest way to do this is using the tidy() function from the broom package:

tidy(logit_model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  term               estimate std.error statistic     p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                 <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)           0.362     0.379     -2.68     7.37e-3    0.165     0.741
2 drug_dose_z          14.7       0.493      5.45     5.08e-8    5.91     41.2  
3 mouse_strainBlack6   27.1       1.15       2.87     4.15e-3    3.94    554.   
4 mouse_strainCD1       4.57      0.500      3.04     2.38e-3    1.80     13.0  


Both drug_dose_z and mouse_strain have p values well below 0.05, so we can reject the null hypothesis for each: a one standard deviation increase in dose is associated with roughly a 13-fold increase in the odds of responding (95% CI approximately 5- to 36-fold), holding strain constant. Relative to the BALBc reference strain, Black6 and CD1 mice both have substantially higher odds of responding at the same dose.






ImportantPractice exercise: modelling a long tail



Let’s use what we have learnt to model the relationship between having a long tail (tail_length_mm is above the median) and the initial weight of the mice, with mouse_strain and sex as covariates.

Starting from dosage, create a new data frame called dosage_ex with a long_tail column (1 if tail_length_mm is above the median, 0 otherwise), and a standardised initial_weight_z column (using scale()).
Before fitting any model, cross-tabulate mouse_strain against long_tail. What do you notice about one of the strains? Why would including mouse_strain as a predictor in a glm() here cause a problem?
Considering your answer to the previous question, fit an appropriate logistic regression model.
Convert the coefficients to odds ratios with and interpret both the initial_weight_z and sex odds ratios in plain language.



Solution

First, create the new columns:

dosage_ex <- dosage %>%
  na.omit(tail_length_mm, initial_weight_g) %>%
  mutate(
     long_tail = case_when(
      tail_length_mm > median(tail_length_mm) ~ 1,
      tail_length_mm < median(tail_length_mm) ~ 0,
      .default = NA),
    initial_weight_z = as.numeric(scale(initial_weight_g))
  )

Then, make the table:

table(dosage_ex$mouse_strain, dosage_ex$long_tail)

        
           0   1
  BALBc   11  48
  Black6 117   0
  CD1     33 110


The table reveals perfect separation: every single Black6 mouse falls in the short-tail group (0 long-tailed Black6 mice). Including mouse_strain as a predictor of long_tail would therefore make the model unstable (an infinite/unreliable coefficient for Black6), so it must be left out of this particular model.
We therefore fit the following model:

ex_logit <- glm(long_tail ~ initial_weight_z + sex, data = dosage_ex, family = "binomial")
tidy(ex_logit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 3 × 7
  term             estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>               <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         0.411     0.190     -4.69 2.78e- 6    0.280     0.591
2 initial_weight_z    0.407     0.143     -6.27 3.70e-10    0.305     0.535
3 sexmale             5.69      0.290      6.00 1.98e- 9    3.28     10.2  


Both initial_weight_z and sex are significant predictors: each 1-SD increase in starting weight is associated with roughly a 59% decrease in the odds of having a long tail (OR ≈ 0.41), while male mice have roughly 6-fold higher odds of a long tail than female mice (OR ≈ 6.2), holding starting weight constant.

title: 21  Further Reading
text:
21.3 Other topics to explore






NoteWhere to go next




Effect sizes: a p value tells you whether an effect exists, but not how big it is. Cohen’s d (for t-tests), eta-squared (for ANOVA) and Cramér’s V (for chi-squared) are standard ways to quantify the size of an effect, independent of sample size the effectsize package is a good place to start.
Repeated measures and mixed-effects models: every test in workshop 6 assumes independent observations, but biological data often isn’t (e.g. multiple measurements from the same mouse, or mice from the same litter/cage). Mixed-effects models (via the lme4 or nlme packages) let you account for this kind of clustering directly in the model.
Predicted probabilities and marginal effects: for logistic (and other) regression models, it’s often more intuitive to talk about a predicted probability than a raw coefficient or odds ratio. The ggeffects package’s ggpredict() function and the emmeans package are both great tools for this, and for comparing predictions between groups while holding other variables constant.
Checking model assumptions visually: rather than checking each assumption one at a time, the performance package’s check_model() function produces a full set of diagnostic plots (residuals, normality, homoscedasticity, multicollinearity and more) for a linear or logistic regression model in a single line of code.
Sample size and power: before you even collect your data, it’s helpful to know how many samples you need to reliably detect an effect of a certain size. The base R power.t.test() function and the pwr package can help answer this for many of the tests covered in workshop 6.
